title: Organization.
heading: 1.1 Organization.
start_phrase: MGM Resorts International (together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated or unless the context requires otherwise,the “Company”) is a Delaware corporation that acts largely as a holding company and, through subsidiaries, owns and operates casino resorts.
summary:
- Overview of MGM Resorts International as a Delaware holding company that owns and operates integrated casino, hotel, and entertainment resorts.
- Portfolio summary:
  - Las Vegas resorts: Bellagio, MGM Grand Las Vegas (including management of The Signature), The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM (rebranded from Monte Carlo in May 2018), Excalibur, Circus Circus.
  - U.S. regional properties: MGM Grand Detroit; MGM National Harbor (MD); MGM Springfield (MA, opened Aug 24, 2018); Borgata (NJ); Beau Rivage (Biloxi, MS); Gold Strike (Tunica, MS).
  - Other assets: The Park dining/entertainment district; Shadow Creek, Primm Valley, and Fallen Oak golf courses.
- MGM Growth Properties LLC (MGP) structure and relationship:
  - UPREIT with assets and operations in MGM Growth Properties Operating Partnership LP.
  - Two share classes: Class A (public) and a single Class B (held by MGM Resorts) with majority voting power so long as MGM’s economic interest threshold is met.
  - Operating Partnership units exchangeable into MGP Class A shares or cash at MGP’s option via independent conflicts committee.
  - Ownership at Dec 31, 2018: MGM owned 73.3% of Operating Partnership units; MGP held 26.7%.
  - Master lease under which MGM (tenant) leases real estate of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor from MGP (landlord).
- 2018–2019 transactions and developments:
  - July 2018: MGP acquired Northfield Park (Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park); Hard Rock continues to manage.
  - Sept 2018: MGM agreed to acquire Northfield’s operating assets from MGP and add to master lease (expected close H1 2019).
  - Jan 2019: MGM acquired Empire City Casino operations and real property; MGP purchased the developed real property and leased it back via the master lease.
  - Aug 2018: MGM and its JV partner sold their 50% interest in Grand Victoria (Elgin, IL).
- International operations:
  - MGM China: approximately 56% controlling interest; owns MGM Grand Paradise; operates MGM Macau and MGM Cotai (opened Feb 13, 2018) with related gaming subconcession and land concessions.
- Joint ventures:
  - CityCenter (50% owned and managed by MGM; 50% by Dubai World affiliate): includes ARIA and Vdara; sold Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas and adjacent retail parcels on Aug 30, 2018.
  - Las Vegas Arena Company (T-Mobile Arena): MGM and AEG each 42.5%, Athena Arena 15%; MGM manages the arena and leases MGM Grand Garden Arena to the venture.
- Segment reporting change:
  - In Q4 2018, operations realigned into three reportable segments: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China.
- Basis of presentation and significant accounting policies:
  - Consolidation principles for wholly- and partially-owned entities; equity method for unconsolidated affiliates with significant influence; elimination of intercompany balances.
  - Variable interest entity (VIE) assessment and primary beneficiary criteria.
  - MGP determined to be a VIE; MGM is the primary beneficiary due to voting control via the Class B share and rights tied to exchangeable OP units; MGP consolidated with its noncontrolling interest recognized.
  - As of Dec 31, 2018, consolidated MGP had approximately $11.0 billion in assets (primarily real estate) and $5.1 billion in liabilities (primarily debt).
text:
1
—
ORGANIZATION
 
Organization.
MGM  Resorts International (together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated or unless the context requires otherwise,the “Company”) is a Delaware 
corporation that acts largely as a holding company and, through subsidiaries, owns and operates casino resorts. 
The
 Company owns and operates the following integrated casino, hotel and entertainment resorts in Las Vegas, Nevada: Bellagio, MGM Grand Las Vegas,The
 Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM (which was branded as Monte Carlo prior to May 2018), Excalibur and Circus Circus LasVegas.
 Operations at MGM Grand Las Vegas include management of The Signature at MGM Grand Las Vegas, a condominium-hotel consisting of three towers.The
 Company  operates  and,  along  with  local  investors,  owns  MGM  Grand  Detroit  in  Detroit,  Michigan,  MGM  National  Harbor  in  Prince  George’s  County,Maryland
 and  MGM  Springfield  in  Springfield,  Massachusetts,  which  opened  on  August  24,  2018.  The  Company  also  owns  and  operates  Borgata  located  onRenaissance
 Pointe in the Marina area of Atlantic City, New Jersey and the following resorts in Mississippi: Beau Rivage in Biloxi and Gold Strike in Tunica.Additionally,
 the Company owns the Park, a dining and entertainment district located between New York-New York and Park MGM, Shadow Creek, an exclusiveworld-class
 golf course located approximately ten miles north of its Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Primm Valley Golf Club at the California/Nevada state line and FallenOak golf course in Saucier, Mississ
ippi. 
MGM
 Growth Properties LLC (“MGP”), a consolidated subsidiary of the Company, is organized as an umbrella partnership REIT (commonly referred to asan
 UPREIT) structure in which substantially all of its assets are owned by and substantially all of its businesses are conducted through MGM Growth PropertiesOperating
 Partnership LP (the “Operating Partnership”). MGP has two classes of authorized and outstanding voting common shares (collectively,  the “shares”):Class A shares and
 a single Class B share. The Company owns MGP’s Class B share, which does not provide its holder any rights to profits or losses or any rights toreceive
 distributions from operations of MGP or upon liquidation or winding up of MGP. MGP’s Class A shareholders are entitled to one vote per share, while theCompany,
 as the owner of the Class B share, is entitled to an amount of votes representing a majority of the total voting power of MGP’s shares so long as theCompany
 and its controlled affiliates’ (excluding MGP) aggregate beneficial ownership of the combined economic interests in MGP and the Operating Partnershipdoes
 not fall below 30%. The Company and MGP each hold Operating Partnership units representing limited partner interests in the Operating Partnership. Thegeneral
 partner of the Operating Partnership is a wholly-owned subsidiary of MGP. The Operating Partnership units held by the Company are exchangeable intoClass
 A shares  of MGP on a one-to-one  basis, or cash at the  fair  value  of a Class  A share.  The determination  of  settlement  method  is at the  option of MGP’sindependent
 conflicts committee. The Company and MGP’s ownership interest percentage in the Operating Partnership have varied based upon the transactions thatMGP
 has  completed,  as  discussed  in  Note  12.  As  of  December  31,  2018,  the  Company  owned  73.3%  of  the  Operating  Partnership  units,  and  MGP  held  theremaining 26.7% ownership inte
rest in the Operating Partnership.   
Pursuant
 to a master lease agreement between a subsidiary of the Company (the “tenant”) and a subsidiary of the Operating Partnership (the “landlord”), thetenant
 leases the real estate assets of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM GrandDetroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM Nation
al Harbor from the landlord. 
In
 July 2018, MGP acquired the membership interests of Northfield Park Associates, LLC (“Northfield”), an Ohio limited liability company that owns thereal
 estate assets and operations of the Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park from Milstein Entertainment LLC. Simultaneously with the close of the transaction,MGP entered into
 a new agreement with an affiliate of Hard Rock Café International (STP), Inc. to continue to serve as the manager of the property. Refer to Note 4for additional information.
 
In
 September 2018, the Company entered into an agreement with MGP to acquire all of the operating assets of Northfield from MGP. Northfield will beadded
 to  the  existing  master  lease  between  the  Company  and  MGP.  The  transaction  is  expected  to  close  in  the  first  half  of  2019,  subject  to  customary  closingconditions. Refer to Note 4 for add
itional information. 
In
 January 2019, the Company acquired the real property and operations associated with the Empire City Casino's race track and casino ("Empire City").MGP
 then  acquired  the  developed  real  property  associated  with  Empire  City  from  the  Company  and  the  real  estate  assets  of  Empire  City  will  be  leased  to  theCompany pursuant to an amendment 
to the master lease. Refer to Note 4 for additional information.   
60
 The
 Company has an approximate 56% controlling interest in MGM China, which owns MGM Grand Paradise, S. A.  (“MGM Grand Paradise”). MGMGrand
 Paradise owns and operates the MGM Macau resort and casino and MGM Cotai, an integrated casino, hotel and entertainment resort located on the CotaiStrip in Macau that opened on Febru
ary 13, 2018, as well as the related gaming subconcession and land conc essions. 
The Company owns 50% of
 and manages CityCenter Holdings, LLC (“CityCenter”), located between Bellagio and Park MGM. The other 50% of CityCenteris
 owned by Infinity World Development Corp, a wholly owned subsidiary of Dubai World, a Dubai, United Arab Emirates government decree entity. CityCenterconsists of Aria, an integrated casino, hotel and entertainment resort; and Vdara
, a luxury condominium-hotel. On August 30, 2018, CityCenter completed the sale ofthe Mandarin Oriental Las Veg
as (“Mandarin Oriental”) and adjacent retail parcels. See Note 6 and Note 17 for additional information related to CityCenter. 
The Company and a subsidiary of Ansch
utz Entertainment Group, Inc. (“AEG”) each own 42.5% of the Las Vegas Arena Company, LLC (“Las Vegas ArenaCompany”),
 the  entity  which  owns  the  T-Mobile  Arena,  and  Athena  Arena,  LLC  owns  the  remaining  15%.  The  Company  also  manages  the  T-Mobile  Arena.Additionally, the Compan
y leases the MGM Grand Garden Arena, located adjacent to the MGM Grand Las Vegas, to the Las Vegas Arena Company. See Note 6 foradditional informat
ion regarding the Company’s investment in the Las Vegas Arena Company. 
In
 August 2018, the Company, along with its joint venture partner, completed the sale of its 50% interest in Grand Victoria, a riverboat casino in Elgin,Illinois. See Note 6 for addit
ional information regarding the Company’s investment in Grand Victoria. 
During
 the  fourth  quarter  of  2018,  the  Company  has  changed  the  aggregation  of  its  operations  into  three  reportable  segments:  Las  Vegas  Strip  Resorts,Regional
 Operations  and  MGM  China.  This  change  of  reportable  segments  reflects  realignment  within  the  Company  stemming  from  the  expansion  of  theCompany’s regional operations. Se
e Note 16 for additional information about the Company’s segments.

title: Principles of consolidation.
heading: 2.1 Principles of consolidation.
start_phrase: For entities not determined to be a variable interest entity (“VIE”), the Company consolidates such entities in which the Company owns 100% of the equity.
summary:
- The Company holds a ~56% controlling interest in MGM China, which owns MGM Grand Paradise, operating MGM Macau and MGM Cotai (opened February 13, 2018), along with related gaming subconcession and land concessions in Macau.
- The Company owns 50% and manages CityCenter Holdings, LLC; the other 50% is owned by Dubai World’s subsidiary. CityCenter includes Aria and Vdara. On August 30, 2018, CityCenter sold the Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas and adjacent retail parcels.
- The Company and AEG each own 42.5% of Las Vegas Arena Company, which owns T-Mobile Arena; Athena Arena owns the remaining 15%. The Company manages T-Mobile Arena and leases MGM Grand Garden Arena to the Las Vegas Arena Company.
- In August 2018, the Company and its joint venture partner sold their 50% interest in the Grand Victoria riverboat casino in Elgin, Illinois.
- In Q4 2018, the Company reorganized into three reportable segments: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China, reflecting expansion of regional operations.
- Basis of presentation and consolidation policies: the Company consolidates entities it controls (including certain less-than-100% owned entities), applies the equity method to unconsolidated affiliates where it has significant influence or joint control, and eliminates intercompany balances.
- Variable interest entity (VIE) framework: the Company identifies and consolidates VIEs where it is the primary beneficiary (has power over significant activities and exposure to significant benefits or losses), reassessing upon changes in facts or arrangements.
- MGP is deemed a VIE; the Company is the primary beneficiary due to majority voting power via a Class B share and rights from exchangeable Operating Partnership units, so it consolidates MGP. MGP’s 26.7% Operating Partnership interest is recorded as noncontrolling interest. As of December 31, 2018, MGP had $11.0 billion in total assets (primarily real estate) and $5.1 billion in total liabilities (primarily indebtedness).
text:
Principles

of
consolidation.
For  entities  not  determined  to  be  a  variable  interest  entity  (“VIE”),  the  Company  consolidates  such  entities  in  which  theCompany
 owns 100% of the equity. For entities in which the Company owns less than 100% of the equity interest, the Company consolidates the entity if it has thedirect
 or indirect ability to control the entities’ activities based upon the terms of the respective entities’ ownership agreements. For these entities, the Companyrecords
 a  noncontrolling  interest  in  the  consolidated  balance  sheets.  The  Company’s  investments  in  unconsolidated  affiliates  which  are  50%  or  less  owned  areaccounted
 for  under  the  equity  method  when  the  Company  can  exercise  significant  influence  over  or  has  joint  control  of  the  unconsolidated  affiliate.  Allintercompany balances 
and transactions are eliminated in consolidation.The Company
 evaluates entities for which control is achieved through means other than voting rights to determine if it is the primary beneficiary of a VIE. AVIE
 is an entity in which either (i) the equity investors as a group, if any, lack the power through voting or similar rights to direct the activities of such entity thatmost
 significantly impact such entity’s economic performance or (ii) the equity investment at risk is insufficient to finance that entity’s activities without additionalsubordinated financial support. The 
Company identifies the primary beneficiary of a VIE as the enterprise that has both of the following characteristics: (i) the powerto
 direct the activities of the VIE that most significantly impact the entity’s economic performance; and (ii) the obligation to absorb losses or receive benefits of theVIE
 that could potentially be significant to the entity. The Company consolidates its investment in a VIE when it determines that it is its primary beneficiary. Forthese
 VIEs, the Company records a noncontrolling interest in the consolidated balance sheets. The Company may change its original assessment of a VIE uponsubsequent
 events such as the modification of contractual arrangements that affect the characteristics or adequacy of the entity’s equity investments at risk and thedisposition of all or a port
ion of an interest held by the primary beneficiary. The Company performs this analysis on an ongoing basis.Management
 has determined that MGP is a VIE because the Class A equity investors as a group lack the power through voting or similar rights to direct theactivities
 of such entity that most significantly impact such entity’s economic performance. The Company has determined that it is the primary beneficiary of MGPand
 consolidates MGP because (i) its ownership of MGP’s single Class B share entitles it to a majority of the total voting power of MGP’s shares, and (ii) theexchangeable
 nature of the Operating Partnership units owned provide the Company the right to receive benefits from MGP that could potentially be significant toMGP.
 The  Company  has  recorded  MGP’s  ownership  interest  in  the  Operating  Partnership  of  26.7%  as  of  December  31,  2018  as  noncontrolling  interest  in  theCompany’s
 consolidated financial statements. As of December 31, 2018, on a consolidated basis MGP had total assets of $11.0 billion, primarily related to its realestate investments, and 
total liabilities of $5.1 billion, primarily related to its indebtedness.  61

title: Management’s use of estimates.
heading: 2.2 Management’s use of estimates.
start_phrase: The consolidated financial statements have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.
summary:
- Basis of presentation and estimates: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP; management uses estimates and assumptions affecting asset/liability amounts, contingent items, and revenues/expenses; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Fair value defined as exit price in an orderly transaction, using a hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs). Used for long-lived assets, unconsolidated investments, cost method investments, business combinations, goodwill/intangibles, and certain financial instruments. Level 1/2 inputs used for long-term debt fair value disclosures (Note 9). Level 2/3 inputs used for assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the Northfield and Borgata transactions (Note 4).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Investments and interest-bearing instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market. Book overdrafts recorded as accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit issued to approved customers and gaming promoters after credit checks. As of Dec 31, 2018 and 2017, about 62% and 40% of gross casino receivables were from foreign customers (primarily Asia), exposing the Company to country/region-specific risks. Receivables are non-interest bearing; write-offs when deemed uncollectible; recoveries recognized when received. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific account reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; management believes no unreserved significant concentrations of credit risk existed at Dec 31, 2018.
- Inventories: Primarily food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies; carried at lower of cost or net realizable value. Average cost for food/beverage and supplies; cost method for retail merchandise.
- Property and equipment: Stated at cost; significant amounts recognized at fair value at acquisition dates due to business combinations. Gains/losses on disposals recognized in earnings; maintenance expensed as incurred. Accrued property and equipment within accounts payable of $47 million (2018) and $28 million (2017); construction retention in other long-term liabilities of $2 million (2018) and $34 million (2017).
- Depreciation: Straight-line over estimated useful lives—buildings and improvements (15–40 years), land improvements (10–20 years), furniture and fixtures (3–20 years), equipment (3–15 years).
- Long-lived asset impairment: Classification as held for sale requires an authorized commitment to sell at a reasonable price and active marketing. Held-for-sale assets recorded at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell, estimated via comparable sales, offers, or discounted cash flows. Assets held and used are evaluated for impairment (discussion continues beyond excerpt).

The  consolidated financial statements have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted inthe
 United States of America. These principles require the Company’s management to make est imates  and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assetsand
 liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during thereporting period. Act 
ual results could diffe r from those estimates.

title: Fair value measurements.
heading: 2.3 Fair value measurements.
start_phrase: Fair value measurements affect the Company’s accounting and impairment assessments of its long-lived assets, investments in unconsolidated affiliates, cost method investments, assets acquired and liabilities assumed in an acquisition, and goodwill and other intangible assets.
summary:
- Basis of presentation and use of estimates: Financial statements prepared under US GAAP; management makes estimates and assumptions affecting reported assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and contingencies; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Definition of fair value and hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs for similar assets, Level 3 unobservable inputs). Fair value impacts accounting for long‑lived assets, investments in unconsolidated affiliates, cost method investments, acquisition accounting, goodwill and intangibles, and certain financial instruments. Company used Level 1 and 2 for long‑term debt fair value disclosures (Note 9) and Level 2 and 3 in measuring assets and liabilities in the Northfield and Borgata acquisitions (Note 4).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Include investments and interest‑bearing instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market; book overdrafts from cash management recorded as accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit issued after background checks; significant concentration of receivables from foreign (primarily Asian) customers (about 62% at Dec 31, 2018; 40% at Dec 31, 2017), with related collectability risk. Receivables are non‑interest bearing, recorded at cost, written off when uncollectible, with recoveries recognized when received. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; management believes no unreserved significant concentrations at Dec 31, 2018.

The
 Company evaluates its investments in unconsolidated affiliates for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carryingvalue of its investment 
may have experienced an “other-than-temporary” decline in value. If such conditions exist, the Company compares the estimated fair value ofthe

 of all relevant factors, including consideration of the Company’s intent and ability to retain its investment. The Company estimates fair value using adiscounted cash flow analysis based on estimated

Goodwill

and
other
intangible
assets.
Goodwill  represents  the  excess  of  purchase  price  over  fair  market  value  of  net  assets  acquired  in  businesscombinations.
 Goodwill  and  indefinite-lived  intangible  assets  must  be  reviewed  for  impairment  at  least  annually  and  between  annual  test  dates  in  certaincircumstances. The
 Company performs its annual impairment tests in the fourth quarter of each fiscal year. No impairments were indicated  or recorded as a result ofthe annual impairmen
t review for goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets in 2018, 2017 and 2016.  
Accounting guidance provides entities the option to perform a qualitative assessment of good
will and indefinite-lived intangible assets (commonly referred toas
 “step zero”) in order to determine whether further impairment testing is necessary. In performing the step zero analysis the Company considers macroeconomicconditions,
 industry  and  market  considerations,  current  and  forecasted  financial  performance,  entity-specific  events,  and changes  in the  composition  or  carryingamount
 of  net  assets  of  reporting  units  for  goodwill.  In  addition,  the  Company  takes  into  consideration  the  amount  of  excess  of  fair  value  over  carrying  valuedetermined
 in the last quantitative analysis that was performed, as well as the period of time that has passed since the last quantitative analysis. If the step zeroanalysis indicates tha
t it is more likely than not that the fair value is less than its carrying amount, the entity would proceed to a quantitative analysis. 
Under
 the quantitative analysis, goodwill for relevant reporting units is tested for impairment using a discounted cash flow analysis based on the estimatedfuture
 results of the Company’s reporting  units discounted using market  discount rates and market indicators  of terminal  year capitalization  rates, and a marketapproach
 that utilizes business enterprise value multiples based on a range of multiples from the Company’s peer group. Effective January 1, 2017, the Companyadopted
 accounting guidance that simplifies goodwill impairment testing by eliminating the requirement to calculate the implied fair value of goodwill (formerly“Step
 2”) in the event that impairment is identified. Instead, an impairment charge is recognized for the amount by which the carrying value exceeds the reportingunit’s
 fair value, not to exceed the total amount of goodwill allocated to that reporting unit. Under the quantitative analysis, license rights are tested for impairmentusing
 a  discounted  cash  flow  approach,  and  trademarks  are  tested  for  impairment  using  the  relief-from-royalty  method.  If  the  fair  value  of  an  indefinite-livedintangible asset is less 
than its carrying amount, an impairment loss is recognized equal to the difference.

title: Revenue recognition.
heading: 2.11 Revenue recognition.
start_phrase: The Company’s revenue from contracts with customers consists of casino wagers transactions, hotel room sales, food and beverage transactions, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.
summary:
- Long-lived assets impairment: Reviewed when indicators arise. Compare undiscounted future cash flows to carrying value; if insufficient, record impairment based on fair value (typically discounted cash flows). Include remaining construction costs for in-development assets. All impairment losses recorded in operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Capitalize interest on major development/construction using project-specific debt or the weighted-average borrowing cost when no specific debt exists. Capitalization stops when a project is substantially complete or development is suspended beyond a brief period.
- Investments in unconsolidated affiliates (equity method): Carrying value adjusted for share of earnings/losses, amortization of basis differences, and capital contributions/distributions. Distributions exceeding equity earnings treated as return of investment and presented as investing cash inflows. Income/losses, gains, and impairments from these investments classified within operating or non-operating income consistent with their nature and alignment with core operations. Impairment evaluated for other-than-temporary declines using DCF analyses and market multiples, considering intent and ability to hold.
- Goodwill and other intangibles: Annual impairment testing in Q4 and interim when warranted; no impairments in 2016–2018. Optional qualitative (“step zero”) assessment considers macro/industry factors, performance, entity-specific events, and prior valuation headroom. Quantitative tests use DCF and market approaches. From Jan 1, 2017, adopted simplified goodwill impairment (no Step 2); impairment equals excess of carrying amount over fair value, capped at recorded goodwill. License rights tested via DCF; trademarks via relief-from-royalty; recognize impairment if fair value < carrying amount.
- Revenue recognition (ASC 606):
  - Casino: Revenue is net win (gaming wins less losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to MGM China promoters/VIP recorded as reductions of casino revenue. Recognized on a portfolio basis by gaming day. Allocate transaction price to discretionary comps at stand‑alone selling price (SSP); third‑party comps recognized as operating expense. Loyalty incentives: allocate portion of net win to points/coupons at SSP (net of breakage), defer and recognize on redemption in the providing department; third‑party redemptions reduce the liability and are settled with the third party.
  - Rooms, food & beverage, retail: Transaction price is net customer amount; recognize when goods/services are transferred (over the stay for rooms; at delivery for F&B and retail). Sales/usage-based taxes excluded. Company may act as agent for certain entertainment shows and OTA-arranged rooms.
  - Bundled packages (e.g., rooms with F&B/entertainment/convention): Allocate revenue to each good/service based on relative SSP determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances.
- Contract and contract-related liabilities: Include (1) outstanding chip liability, (2) loyalty program obligations, and (3) customer advances and other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, room/convention deposits, unpaid wagers). Generally recognized as revenue within a year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities. Activity and balances for 2017–2018 are summarized in a table.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services recognized as revenue when incurred (primarily related to CityCenter).
- Revenue by source: Disaggregated by type (casino, room, F&B, entertainment, retail/other) and geography in a referenced note.

63
 The

 on markers, which is estimated based upon historical business practice, and recorded as a reduction of casino revenue. Commissions rebated to gamingpromoters
 and VIP players at MGM China are also recorded as a reduction of casino  revenue. The Company accounts for casino revenue on a portfolio basis giventhe similar chara
cteristics of wagers by recognizing net win per gaming day versus on an individual wager basis. 
For
 casino  wager  transactions  that  include  other  goods  and  services  provided  by  the  Company  to  gaming  patrons  on  a  discretionary  basis  to  incentivizegaming,
 the  Company  allocates  revenue  from  the  casino  wager  transaction  to  the  good  or  service  delivered  based  upon  stand-alone  selling  price  (“SSP”).Discretionary goods and servic
es provided by the Company and supplied by third parties are recognized as an operating expense. 
For
 casino wager transactions that include incentives earned by customers under the Company’s loyalty programs, the Company allocates a portion of netwin based
 upon the SSP of such incentive (less estimated breakage). This allocation is deferred and recognized as revenue when the customer redeems the incentive.When
 redeemed, revenue is recognized in the department that provides the goods or service. Redemption of loyalty incentives at third party outlets are deductedfrom
 the loyalty liability and amounts owed are paid to the third party, with any discount received recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives providedto
 gaming  customers  were  collectively  $2.3  billion,  $2.1  billion  and  $1.8  billion  for  the  years  ended  December  31,  2018,  2017  and  2016,  respectively. After allocating revenue to o
ther goods and services provided as part of casino wager transactions, the Company records the residual amount to casino revenue. 
The
 transaction  price  of  rooms,  food  and  beverage,  and  retail  contracts  is  the  net  amount  collected  from  the  customer  for  such  goods  and  services.  Thetransaction
 price for such contracts is recorded as revenue when the good or service is transferred to the customer over their stay at the hotel or when the delivery ismade for the food & beverage and retail & other contracts. Sales and usage-based taxes are excluded from revenue
s. For some arrangements, the Company acts as anagent
 in that it arranges for another party to transfer goods and services, which primarily include certain of the Company’s entertainment shows as well as customerrooms arranged by online tr
avel agents. 
The
 Company also has other contracts that include multiple goods and services, such as packages that bundle food, beverage, or entertainment offerings withhotel
 stays  and  convention  services.  For  such  arrangements,  the  Company  allocates  revenue  to  each  good  or  service  based  on  its  relative  SSP.  The  Companyprimarily

title: Contract and Contract-Related Liabilities.
heading: 2.12 Contract and Contract-Related Liabilities.
start_phrase: There may be a difference between the timing of cash receipts from the customer and the recognition of revenue, resulting in a contract or contract-related liability.
summary:
- Casino revenue recognition: Transaction price for casino wagers is net win (wins minus losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to gaming promoters/VIP players (e.g., MGM China) reduce casino revenue. Revenue is recognized on a portfolio basis by gaming day.
- Discretionary comps: When wagers include Company-provided discretionary goods/services to incentivize play, revenue is allocated to those items based on their stand-alone selling price (SSP). Comps supplied by third parties are recorded as operating expense.
- Loyalty programs: A portion of net win equal to the SSP of earned incentives (less estimated breakage) is deferred and recognized upon redemption, in the department providing the good/service. Redemptions at third-party outlets reduce the loyalty liability; amounts paid to third parties are settled in cash, and any discount received is recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives to gaming customers totaled $2.3B (2018), $2.1B (2017), and $1.8B (2016). Residual amounts after allocations are recorded as casino revenue.
- Rooms, food & beverage, retail: Transaction price is the net amount collected; revenue is recognized over the hotel stay or upon delivery for F&B and retail. Sales and usage-based taxes are excluded. The Company acts as an agent in certain arrangements (e.g., some entertainment shows and rooms booked via online travel agents).
- Bundled packages: For packages combining rooms with food, beverage, entertainment, or convention services, revenue is allocated to each component based on relative SSP, primarily determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances.
- Contract and contract-related liabilities: Arise from timing differences between cash receipts and revenue recognition and include (1) outstanding chip liability, (2) loyalty program obligations (deferred revenue for incentives), and (3) customer advances and other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, room/convention deposits, unpaid wagers). These are generally recognized as revenue within one year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities.
  - 2018 year-end balances: Outstanding chip liability $323.8M; Loyalty program $113.3M; Customer advances and other $667.3M. Changes in 2018: chip liability decreased $273.9M; loyalty increased $22.2M; customer advances increased $127.7M.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services are recognized as revenue when incurred, primarily related to management of CityCenter.
- Revenue disaggregation: Revenue is presented by source (casino, room, food & beverage, entertainment, retail & other) and by geographic region in a referenced note.

summary:
- Casino revenue recognition: Transaction price is net win (gaming wins less losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to promoters/VIP players reduce casino revenue. Revenue is recognized on a portfolio basis per gaming day. For discretionary comps bundled with wagers, revenue is allocated to the goods/services at stand‑alone selling price (SSP); third‑party comps are expensed.
- Loyalty programs: A portion of net win is allocated to loyalty incentives at SSP net of estimated breakage, deferred, and recognized upon redemption in the providing department. Third‑party redemptions reduce the loyalty liability; amounts paid to third parties are expensed with any discount recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives to gaming customers were $2.3B (2018), $2.1B (2017), $1.8B (2016). Residual amounts after allocations are recorded as casino revenue.
- Non-casino revenue (rooms, food & beverage, retail): Transaction price is the net amount collected. Revenue is recognized over the hotel stay or upon delivery of goods/services; sales and usage‑based taxes are excluded. In certain arrangements the Company acts as an agent (e.g., some entertainment shows and rooms sold via online travel agents).
- Bundled contracts: For packages combining rooms with food, beverage, or entertainment, revenue is allocated to each element based on relative SSP, generally determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances to similar customers.
- Contract and contract‑related liabilities: Three types—outstanding chip liability; loyalty program obligations; and customer advances/other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, deposits on rooms and convention space, unpaid wagers). Generally recognized as revenue within one year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities. Balances: Outstanding chip liability declined to $324M at 12/31/2018 from $598M; loyalty obligations rose to $113M from $91M; customer advances/other rose to $667M from $540M.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services are recognized as revenue when incurred (primarily CityCenter management).
- Revenue disaggregation and lease revenues: Revenue is presented by type (casino, room, F&B, entertainment/retail/other) and geography (Note 16). Lease revenues are classified by the tenant’s activity, including F&B lease revenue of $51M (2018, 2017) and $50M (2016), and entertainment/retail/other lease revenue of $87M (2018), $79M (2017), $77M (2016).
- Advertising: Expensed when first run; expense was $305M (2018), $223M (2017), $171M (2016).
- Corporate expense: Unallocated payroll, aircraft, professional fees, and other non‑property costs, including expenses for evaluating/pursuing new business opportunities (expensed as incurred).
- Preopening and start‑up expenses: Expensed as incurred; include payroll, outside services, advertising, and other start‑up costs.
- Property transactions, net: Includes impairments/write‑downs, demolition costs, and gains/losses on asset sales (see Note 15).
- Redeemable noncontrolling interests (MGM National Harbor): Non‑voting interests receive annual preferred distributions based on a percentage of net gaming revenue, accrued quarterly and paid 90 days after year‑end. Beginning 12/31/2019, holders have put rights; certain early sell‑back rights exist if guarantees/liens are granted by the Company. Classified as mezzanine equity; initially recorded at fair value, then adjusted to the maximum redemption value (not below initial) with changes recorded to additional paid‑in capital; carrying amount also adjusted for accrued preferred distributions, which impact net income attributable to noncontrolling interests.

 “Leases”, (“ASC 842”). ASC 842 is effective for fiscal years, and interim periods within those years, beginning after December 15, 2018. ASC 842 requires adual
 approach  for  lessee  accounting  under  which  a  lessee  would  classify  and  account  for  its  lease  agreements  as  either  finance  or  operating.  Both  finance  andoperating
 leases will result in the lessee recognizing a right-of-use (“ROU”) asset and a corresponding lease liability. For finance leases, the lessee will recognizeinterest

 period financial information. The Company will elect the basket of transition practical expedients which includes not needing to reassess: (1) whetherany
 expired or existing contracts are or contain leases, (2) the lease classification for any expired or existing leases, and (3) direct costs for any existing leases. TheCompany

title: Empire City
heading: 4.2 Empire City
start_phrase: On January 29, 2019, the Company acquired the real property and operations associated with the Empire City Casino's race track and casino (“Empire City”)for total consideration of approximately $864 million, plus customary working capital and other adjustments (“Empire City Acquisition”).
summary:
- Empire City acquisition: On January 29, 2019, the Company acquired Empire City Casino’s racetrack and casino for approximately $864 million plus customary adjustments. Consideration included assumption of ~$246 million of debt (subsequently repaid), issuance of ~$266 million in common stock, and the remainder in cash. There is contingent consideration of $50 million if a live table games license is awarded by December 31, 2022 and accepted by December 31, 2024. Preliminary purchase accounting is not yet complete. Post-closing, MGP acquired the developed real property and leases it back to a Company subsidiary.

- Borgata acquisition: On August 1, 2016, the Company acquired Boyd Gaming’s ownership interest in Borgata for $604 million in cash, after which MGP acquired Borgata’s real property and leased it back to a Company subsidiary. Borgata entered into a property tax reimbursement agreement in February 2017 with New Jersey’s Department of Community Affairs and Atlantic City, receiving $72 million in June 2017, half of which was paid to Boyd Gaming net of fees. The transaction resulted in the Company obtaining 100% ownership, consolidating Borgata as of August 1, 2016, and recognizing assets and liabilities at fair value. The pre-existing 50% equity method stake was remeasured, implying a total Borgata equity value of approximately $1.2 billion and a $430 million step-acquisition gain. Borgata’s results from August 1 to December 31, 2016 were: net revenue $350 million, operating income $34 million, and net income $4 million.

- Pro forma information: Unaudited pro forma results assuming control as of January 1, 2015 (excluding the $430 million gain) for the year ended December 31, 2016 show net revenues of $9,963,322 thousand, net income attributable to MGM Resorts International of $818,247 thousand, basic EPS of $1.44, and diluted EPS of $1.43.

Swaps designated as cash flow hedges.

Term loans amortize 5% of original principal quarterly from September 2018 through December 2021, with the balance due March 2022. 2018 repayments: $507 million of term loans. amount of the term loan A outstanding as of the amendment effective date. 
Prior
 to the amendment, the term loan A facility was subject to amortization in equal quarterly installments of 2.5% of the initial aggregate principal amountto be payable each year. Th
e Operating Partnership permanently repaid $4 million of the term loan A facility for the year ended December 31, 2018. The term loan Bfacility
 is subject to equal quarterly installments of 1.0% of the initial aggregate principal amount to be payable each year. The Operating Partnership permanentlyrepaid
 $19 million of the term loan B facility for the year ended December 31, 2018, in accordance with the scheduled amortization. At December 31, 2018, $550million was
 drawn on the revolving credit facility. At December 31, 2018, the interest rates on the term loan A facility and the term loan B facility were both 4.52%,and the interest rat
e on the revolving credit facility was 4.43%.

 maximum total net debt to adjusted assets ratio and a minimum interest coverage ratio. The Operating Partnership was in compliance with its creditfacility covenants a
t December 31, 2018.  
The
 Operating Partnership senior credit facility is guaranteed by each of the Operating Partnership’s existing and subsequently acquired direct and indirectwholly
 owned material domestic restricted subsidiaries, and secured by a first priority lien security interest on substantially all of the Operating Partnership’s andsuch restricted subsidia
ries’ material assets, including mortgages on its real estate, excluding the real estate assets of MGM National Harbor and Empire City, subjectto customary exclusions.
 
The
 Operating Partnership is party to interest rate swaps to mitigate the interest rate risk inherent in its senior secured term loan B facility. As of December31,
 2018, the Operating Partnership pays a weighted average fixed rate of 1.844% on total notional amount of $1.2 billion and the variable rate received resetsmonthly
 to the one-month LIBOR with no minimum  floor. In December  2018, the Operating Partnership  entered  into additional  interest  rate swaps that have anotional

 0%. Such interest rate swaps will become effective on December 31, 2019. As of December 31, 2018 and 2017, the derivative financial instruments have beendesignated as cash flow hedges and qu
alify for hedge accounting.

summary:

- Details the Operating Partnership’s senior secured credit facility at December 31, 2018: $470 million term loan A, $1.8 billion term loan B, and $1.35 billion revolver. Notes 2018 repricing and extensions (term loan B to LIBOR + 2.00% and maturity to March 2025; revolver increased by $750 million to $1.35 billion; term loan A increased by $200 million; both revolver and term loan A repriced to LIBOR + 1.75%–2.25% with maturities to June 2023). Amortization changes include term loan A quarterly payments of 0.625% starting September 30, 2019; term loan B 1% annual amortization. 2018 repayments: $4 million (A) and $19 million (B). Notes guarantees by material domestic restricted subsidiaries and first-lien security on substantially all material assets, including real estate mortgages, excluding MGM National Harbor and Empire City.

title: INCOME TAXES
heading: NOTE 10 — INCOME TAXES
start_phrase: The Company recognizes deferred income tax assets, net of applicable reserves, related to net operating losses, tax credit carryforwards and certaintemporary differences.
summary:
- Debt facilities and compliance:
  - MGM China’s credit facility includes standard reps and warranties, events of default, and covenants, including maximum leverage and minimum interest coverage; MGM China was in compliance as of December 31, 2018.

- Parent company senior notes activity:
  - Repaid $850 million 8.625% notes due 2019 in February 2019.
  - Issued $1.0 billion of 5.750% senior notes due 2025 in June 2018.
  - Redeemed $475 million of 11.375% notes due 2018 in July 2017, incurring a $30 million loss on early retirement.

- Operating Partnership senior notes:
  - Issued $350 million of 4.50% notes due 2028 in September 2017.
  - Issued $750 million of 5.75% notes due 2027 in January 2019.
  - Notes are fully and unconditionally guaranteed on a senior basis by certain subsidiaries (other than the co-issuer). Redemption terms include par plus make-whole (if prior to three months before maturity), plus accrued interest. Indentures include customary covenants and events of default, with exceptions including unlimited restricted payments to maintain MGP’s REIT status.

- Long-term debt:
  - Maturity schedule at December 31, 2018 totals $15.253 billion, with principal due by year: 2019 $1.273b; 2020 $1.966b; 2021 $1.716b; 2022 $2.306b; 2023 $2.885b; thereafter $5.107b.
  - Estimated fair value of long-term debt: $15.1 billion (2018) and $13.6 billion (2017), based on quoted market prices.

- Income taxes overview:
  - Deferred tax assets recognized for NOLs, credits, and temporary differences, subject to valuation allowances; benefits recognized when more likely than not.
  - Income (loss) before taxes by geography (2016–2018) presented, showing primarily domestic income and variable foreign results.
  - Detailed tax provision/benefit by federal, state, and foreign components for 2016–2018 and effective tax rate reconciliations, highlighting key drivers such as Tax Act impacts, foreign rates, credits, Macau dividend tax, and valuation allowances.
  - Net deferred tax liability totaled approximately $1.343 billion at December 31, 2018, with major liabilities for property and equipment and intangibles; significant federal/state and foreign deferred tax asset and liability components disclosed.

- U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act) impacts:
  - Summary of major provisions (rate reduction to 21%, transition tax, GILTI, interest and compensation limitations, bonus depreciation, etc.).
  - SAB 118 measurement period applied: recorded a provisional $1.4 billion non-cash net tax benefit in 2017 ($988 million from rate reduction; $438 million from FTC valuation allowance reassessment). No transition tax expense due to FTC offsets.
  - Measurement period finalized in 2018: recorded $20 million non-cash tax expense from FTC-related valuation allowance adjustments and finalized treatment of certain fringe benefits (immaterial).
  - GILTI accounted for as current period expense when incurred; no deferred tax recorded for future GILTI.

- Foreign tax credits (FTCs) and valuation allowances:
  - $2.9 billion FTC carryover as of December 31, 2018, primarily from Macau Special Gaming Tax; $2.4 billion valuation allowance recorded, resulting in a $481 million net FTC deferred tax asset.
  - Expect limited new FTC generation under the Tax Act; utilization dependent on foreign source income and recapture of $1.7 billion overall domestic losses.
  - FTC expirations: $640m (2022), $976m (2023), $782m (2024), $332m (2025), $196m (2027). Significant judgment involved; changes could materially affect the valuation allowance and tax provision.

- Macau tax matters:
  - MGM Grand Paradise’s gaming profits exempt from 12% complementary tax through March 31, 2020. Without the exemption, net income would have decreased by $43 million (2018) and $38 million (2017).
  - Post-March 31, 2020, the company assumes payment of the 12% tax on gaming profits for deferred tax measurement.
  - Non-gaming operations subject to complementary tax; $866 million non-gaming NOL carryforward at December 31, 2018 expiring 2019–2021.
  - Dividend distributions: annual fee arrangement to settle 12% complementary tax on distributions for profits earned through December 31, 2016; extended on March 15, 2018 to cover profits earned January 1, 2017–March 31, 2020 (approximately $1 million per year for 2017–2019 and $0.3 million for Q1 2020). Reversal of previously recorded $41 million deferred tax on 2017 earnings reduced 2018 tax provision, partially offset by the annual payment.

- Other NOLs and valuation allowances:
  - State NOLs of $355 million at December 31, 2018 (DTAs of $23 million), expiring 2029–2038; $3 million valuation allowance on certain state DTAs.
  - $26 million valuation allowance on certain Macau DTAs and $2 million on Hong Kong NOLs.

- Unrecognized tax benefits and audits:
  - Gross unrecognized tax benefits increased to $24.5 million at December 31, 2018; $13 million would affect the effective tax rate if recognized. Interest and penalties immaterial; no material change expected within 12 months.
  - Tax filings across U.S. federal, state, local, and foreign jurisdictions; 2014 U.S. consolidated return under IRS examination. CityCenter’s 2014 IRS exam completed in 2018 with immaterial impact.
  - State exams ongoing: Mississippi and New Jersey (2014–2016), Michigan (2014–2017). Earlier periods generally closed, subject to NOL utilization adjustments.

- Commitments and contingencies:
  - Leases: company leases real estate and equipment under operating and some capital leases, with certain leases including indexed or appraisal-based rent escalations.

On December 22, 2017, the U.S. government enac
ted comprehensive tax legislation commonly referred to as the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Tax Act”).The Tax
 Act makes broad and complex changes to the U.S. tax code that are generally applicable to tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, including, but notlimited
 to,  (1)  reducing  the  U.S.  federal  corporate  tax  rate  from  35  percent  to  21  percent;  (2)  requiring  companies  to  pay  a  one-time  transition  tax  on  certainunrepatriated earnings of foreign subsidiaries; (3) generally eliminating U.
S. federal income taxes on dividends from foreign subsidiaries; (4) adding a new provisiondesigned
 to tax global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI), which allows for the possibility of using foreign tax credits (FTCs) and a deduction of up to 50 percentto offset
 the income tax liability (subject to some limitations); (5) creating a new limitation on deductible interest expense; (6) imposing additional limitations on thedeductibility of executive compensation and certain employee fringe benefits; and (7) increasing bon
us depreciation to allow for full expensing of qualified property. 
The
 SEC staff issued Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (SAB 118), which provides guidance on accounting for the tax effects of the Tax Act. SAB 118provides
 a measurement period that should not extend beyond one year from the Tax Act enactment date for companies to complete the accounting under ASC 740.In accordance with SAB 118, a company must 
reflect the income tax effects of those aspects of the Tax Act for which the accounting under ASC 740 is complete. Tothe
 extent that a company’s accounting for certain income tax effects of the Tax Act is incomplete but it is able to determine a reasonable estimate, it must record aprovisional estimate in the financial statements. If a company cannot determine a provisional estimate to be included in the financial statements, it sho
uld continue toapply ASC 740 on the basis of the provisions of the 
tax laws that were in effect immediately before the enactment of the Tax Act.  79
  
The
 Company’s  accounting  for  certain  elements  of  the  Tax  Act  was  incomplete  as  of  December  31,  2017.  However,  the  Company  was  able  to  makereasonable estimates
 of certain effects and, therefore, recorded a provisional discrete non-cash net tax benefit of $1.4 billion in the period ended December 31, 2017,consisting
 of a benefit of $988 million for the corporate rate reduction and a benefit of $438 million from its provisional re-assessment of the Tax Act’s impact onthe
 valuation allowance on its foreign tax credit (“FTC”) carryovers. The Company did not provide tax expense for the transition tax on its unrepatriated earnings,which totaled $669 million withou
t regard to actual 2017 distributions of $62 million, because such earnings were fully offset by FTCs. 
The
 Company’s accounting for the impact of the Tax Act is now complete. The Company recorded non-cash income tax expense totaling $20 million duringthe measurement
 period in 2018, as it adjusted its valuation allowance on its FTC carryovers to account for guidance clarifying the treatment of FTCs resulting fromGILTI
 and other provisions impacting FTC utilization. These measurement period adjustments increased the Company’s effective tax rate by 3% during the yearended
 December 31, 2018. In addition, the Company finalized its accounting for the tax treatment of indirect costs of providing certain employee fringe benefitssubject
 to limitation under the Tax Act. This measurement period adjustment had an immaterial impact on the effective tax rate for the year ended December 31,2018.
 
The
 Company has made an accounting policy decision to treat taxes due, if any, on future inclusions in U.S. taxable income under the GILTI provisions as acurrent period expense when in
curred. Accordingly, the Company has not provided a deferred tax liability for any GILTI taxes that may result in future periods. 
The
 Company has recorded a valuation allowance of $2.4 billion on its FTC carryover of $2.9 billion as of December 31, 2018, resulting in an FTC netdeferred
 tax asset of $481 million. The FTCs are attributable to the Macau Special Gaming Tax, which is 35% of gross gaming revenue in Macau. Because MGMGrand
 Paradise is presently exempt from the Macau 12% complementary tax on gaming profits, the Company believes that payment of the Macau Special GamingTax
 qualifies  as  a  tax  paid  in  lieu  of  an  income  tax  that  is  creditable  against  U.S.  taxes.  While  the  Company  generally  does  not  expect  to  generate  new  FTCcarryovers
 under the Tax Act, it will be able to utilize its existing FTC carryovers to the extent that it has active foreign source income during the 10-year FTCcarryforward
 period. Such foreign source income includes the recapture, to the extent of U.S. taxable income, of overall domestic losses that totaled $1.7 billion atDecember 31, 2018. The Compan
y relies on future U.S. source operating income in assessing utilization of the overall domestic losses and, by extension, future FTCrealization
 during the 10-year FTC carryover period. The FTC carryovers will expire if not utilized as follows: $640 million in 2022; $976 million in 2023; $782million in 2024; $332 million 
in 2025; and $196 million in 2027. 
The
 Company’s assessment of the realization of its FTC deferred tax asset is based on available evidence, including assumptions concerning future U.S.operating
 profits and our interpretations of the Tax Act based upon guidance issued to date. As a result, significant judgment is required in assessing the possibleneed
 for a valuation allowance and changes to such assumptions could result in a material change in the valuation allowance with a corresponding impact on theprovision for income taxes 
in the period including such change.   
Income
 generated  from  gaming  operations  of  MGM  Grand  Paradise  is  exempted  from  Macau’s  12%  complementary  tax,  pursuant  to  approval  from  theMacau
 government. Absent this exemption, “Net income attributable to MGM Resorts International” would have decreased by $43 million and $38 million in 2018and 2017, respectively, and dilu
ted earnings per share would have decreased by $0.08 and $0.07 in 2018 and 2017, respectively. 
MGM
 Grand Paradise has been granted an exemption from the Macau 12% complementary tax on gaming profits through March 31, 2020, which is the endof

eyond March 31, 2020 and has factored that assumption into the measurement of Macau deferred tax assets and liabilities. 
Non-gaming
 operations  remain  subject  to  the  Macau  complementary  tax.  MGM  Grand  Paradise  had  at  December  31,  2018  a  complementary  tax  netoperating

MGM

The  Company and/or certain of its subsidiaries have been named as defendants in a number of lawsuits related to the October 1, 2017shooting in Las
 Vegas. The matters involve in large degree the same legal and factual issues, each case being filed on behalf of individuals who are seeking damagesfor
 emotional  distress,  physical  injury,  medical  expenses,  economic  damages  and/or  wrongful  death  based  on  assertions  that  the  Company  and/or  certain  of  itssubsidiaries
 were negligent.  The Company also received  letters  from  attorneys  purporting  to represent  other  persons with claims  related  to the October  1, 2017shooting.
 Lawsuits  were  first  filed  in  October  2017  and  include  actions  filed  by  multiple  individuals  in  the  District  Court  of  Clark  County,  Nevada  and  in  theSuperior
 Court of Los Angeles County, California. Some of the original actions have been voluntarily dismissed, and plaintiffs’ counsel indicate they anticipate re-filing
 the lawsuits in similar form. In June 2018, the Company removed to federal court all actions that remained pending in California and Nevada state courtsfollowing the voluntary dismissals.
 Motions to remand have been filed in several cases, and the Company anticipates that there may be additional motions to remandfiled
 in the future. The Company also initiated declaratory relief actions in federal courts in various districts against individuals who had sued or stated an intent tosue.
 Additional lawsuits related to this incident may be filed in the future. In February of 2019, the Company and plaintiffs’ counsel commenced mediation of thesematters.  The above-descri
bed litigation currently is stayed pending mediation. 
The Company is currently unable to
 reliably predict the future developments in, outcome of, and economic costs and other consequences of pending or futurelitigation related
 to this matter. The Company will continue to investigate the factual and legal defenses, and evaluate these matters based on subsequent events, newinformation
 and future circumstances. The Company intends to defend against these lawsuits and ultimately believes it should prevail, but litigation of this type isinherently
 unpredictable. Although there are significant procedural, factual and legal issues to be resolved that could significantly affect the Company’s belief as tothe
 possibility of liability, the Company currently believes that it is reasonably possible that it could incur liability in connection with certain of these lawsuits. Theforegoing
 determination was made in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, as codified in ASC 450-20, and is not an admission of any liabilityon the part of the Company or any of
 its affiliates. Given that these cases are in the early stages and in light of the uncertainties surrounding them, the Company doesnot
 currently  possess  sufficient  information  to  determine  a  range  of  reasonably  possible  liability.  In  the  event  the  Company  incurs  any  liability,  the  Companybelieves
 it  is  unlikely  it  would  incur  losses  in  connection  with  these  claims  in  excess  of  its  insurance  coverage.  The  insurance  carriers  have  not  expressed  areservation
 of rights  or coverage  defense that  affects  the Company’s evaluation  of potential  losses in connection  with these  claims.  In addition,  the Company’sgeneral
 liability insurance coverage provides, as part of the contractual “duty to defend”, payment of legal fees and associated costs incurred to defend coveredlawsuits
 that are filed arising from the October 1, 2017 shooting in Las Vegas. Payment of such fees and costs is in addition to (and not limited by) the limits of theinsurance policies and 
does not erode the total liability coverage available.

summary:

benefit
plans.
The  Company currently participates in multiemployer pension plans in which the risks of participating differs from single-employer plans in the fol
lowing aspects: 
 
a) Assets contributed to the mul tiemployer plan by one employer may be used to provide benefits to employees of other participating employers; 
b) If a participating employer stops contributing to the plan, the unfunded obligations of the plan may be borne by the remaining participating employers; 
c) If  an entity chooses to stop participating in some of its multiemployer plans, the entity may be required to pay those plans an amount based on theunderfunded status of the plan, 
referred to as a withdrawal liability; and 
d) If  the plan is terminated by withdrawal of all employers and if the value of the nonforfeitable benefits exceeds plan assets and withdrawal liabilitypayments, employers are re
quired by law to make up the insufficient difference.

title: Las Vegas Strip Resorts.

summary:
- Note 16 covers segment information and reporting.
- Management views each casino resort as an operating segment and aggregates them based on similar economics, customers, services/products, regulatory environments, and management/reporting structure.
- In Q4 2018, the Company realigned reportable segments to three groups: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China, reflecting expansion of regional operations.

heading: 17.3 MGM Branding and Development Holdings, Ltd.
start_phrase: MGM Branding and Development Holdings, Ltd. (to gether with its subsidiary MGM Development Services, Ltd., “MGM Branding and Development”), anentity included in the Company’s consolidated financial statements in which Ms. Ho indirectly holds a noncontrolling interest, is party to a brand license agreem ent and a development services agreement with MGM China, for which the related amounts are eliminated in consolidation.
summary:
- Related-party arrangements: MGM Branding and Development Holdings, Ltd. (and subsidiary) has brand license and development services agreements with MGM China; amounts eliminated in consolidation. An entity owned by Ms. Ho (an indirect noncontrolling interest holder) received distributions of $22m (2018), $15m (2017), and $15m (2016).

- MGP master lease overview: Tenant leases the real estate of multiple MGM properties (including The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor) under a triple-net structure.
  - Term: Initial 10-year term starting April 25, 2016, with four 5-year extension options that must apply to all covered real estate. Special term for MGM National Harbor ends April 31, 2024, with renewal mechanics that, if not exercised for National Harbor, also forfeit the right to renew the rest of the properties at the 2026 initial term end.
  - Right of first offer: Landlord has ROFO on MGM Springfield.
  - Rent: Increased to $770m from $757m effective April 1, 2018 (lease year three). Approximately 90% base rent and 10% percentage rent.
  - Escalators: 2% annual increases on base rent through the sixth lease year and potential additional 2% increases thereafter subject to an adjusted net revenue to rent ratio; percentage rent may increase in year six and every five years thereafter based on prior five-year average net revenue.
  - Covenants: Customary events of default and financial covenants; company in compliance as of December 31, 2018.

- Subsequent and related transactions:
  - Empire City: After the January 2019 acquisition, MGP bought the developed real property from the company for ~$634m; added to the master lease, increasing annual rent by $50m (90% fixed with 2% annual growth until 2022). Landlord obtains ROFO on certain adjacent undeveloped land tied to future development.
  - Northfield OpCo: Definitive agreement (Sept 2018) for the company to acquire Northfield OpCo from MGP for ~$275m; its real estate to be leased back via master lease amendment, increasing rent by $60m (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022). Expected close in H1 2019, subject to customary conditions.
  - Park MGM Lease Transaction: December 2018 agreement for MGP to pay $638m for renovations at Park MGM and NoMad Las Vegas; master lease amendment to increase annual rent by $50m (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022). Expected close in Q1 2019, subject to customary conditions.

heading: 17.4 MGP
start_phrase: As further described in Note 1, pursuant to the master lease, the tenant leases the real estate assets of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-NewYork, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunic a, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata and MGM National Harbor from the landlord.
summary:
- Related-party arrangements: MGM Branding and Development Holdings, Ltd. (and subsidiary) has brand license and development services agreements with MGM China; amounts are eliminated in consolidation. An entity indirectly owned by Ms. Ho (a noncontrolling interest holder) received distributions of $22M (2018), $15M (2017), and $15M (2016).

- MGP master lease overview: Tenant leases real estate for The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor. Initial term began April 25, 2016 for 10 years with four 5-year renewal options; triple-net structure. Landlord has a right of first offer on MGM Springfield.

- MGM National Harbor specific terms: Initial term under the master lease ends April 31, 2024; renewal mechanics tied to whether other properties are renewed. If the tenant does not renew National Harbor at that time, it forfeits the right to renew the rest when their initial term ends in 2026.

- Rent mechanics and escalators: Annual rent increased to $770M (from $757M) effective April 1, 2018. Roughly 90% base rent and 10% percentage rent as of Dec 31, 2018. Fixed 2% annual escalators on base rent through the sixth lease year, with potential additional 2% thereafter subject to an adjusted net revenue-to-rent test; percentage rent resets in year six and every five years thereafter based on average net revenue. The lease contains customary covenants; the Company was in compliance as of Dec 31, 2018.

- Subsequent and pending transactions with MGP:
  - Empire City: In Jan 2019, MGP acquired the developed real property for ~$634M; master lease amended to add $50M of annual rent (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); landlord ROFO on certain adjacent undeveloped land if developed and sold.
  - Northfield OpCo: Definitive agreement for the Company to acquire Northfield OpCo from MGP for ~$275M; real estate to be leased under the master lease with a $60M annual rent increase (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); expected close H1 2019.
  - Park MGM Lease Transaction: Agreement for MGP to pay $638M for Park MGM/NoMad Las Vegas renovations; master lease amendment to add $50M annual rent (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); expected close Q1 2019.

- Consolidation and noncontrolling interests: All intercompany transactions, including under the master lease, are eliminated in consolidation. Public ownership of MGP Class A shares is presented as noncontrolling interests.

- Note 18—Condensed consolidating financial information:
  - Debt guarantees: Principal debt is guaranteed by material domestic subsidiaries, excluding MGP and its Operating Partnership, MGM Grand Detroit, MGM National Harbor, MGM Springfield, and their subsidiaries. International subsidiaries, including MGM China, are not guarantors.
  - Presentation: Separate condensed financial information is provided for subsidiary guarantors and non-guarantors as of Dec 31, 2018 and 2017 and for the years ended 2018, 2017, and 2016. Net intercompany account changes are shown as investing or financing activities based on net asset/liability positions.
  - Sale-leaseback accounting: Certain subsidiaries own Operating Partnership units and use the equity method; their continuing involvement means prior sale-leaseback of real estate under the master lease did not qualify as a sale. Those MGM subsidiaries keep the real estate on their balance sheets and record finance liabilities (within other long-term obligations) for lease payments and related interest; the same assets also appear on MGP’s balance sheet, with eliminations reflected in consolidating columns.
  - ASC 842 impact: The Company is reassessing whether the master lease transactions now qualify as a sale and the corresponding lease classification, which could affect the condensed consolidating information.
