 apply to all of the real estate under the master lease at the time of the extension. The master lease has a triple-net structure, which requires the tenant to paysubstantially all
 costs associated with the lease, including real estate taxes, insurance, utilities and routine maintenance, in addition to the base rent. Additionally, themaster lease
 provides the landlord with a right of first offer with respect to MGM Springfield, which the landlord may exercise should the Company elect to sell thisproperty in
 the future. In connection with the MGM National Harbor transaction, the master lease was amended to provide that the initial term with respect to MGMNational
 Harbor ends on April 31, 2024. Thereafter, the initial term of the master lease with respect to MGM National Harbor may be renewed at the option of thetenant for
 an initial renewal period lasting until the earlier of the end of the then-current term of the master lease or the next renewal term (depending on whether theCompany
 elects to renew the other properties under the master lease in connection with the expiration of the initial ten-year term). If, however, the tenant choosesnot to
 renew the lease with respect to MGM National Harbor after the initial MGM National Harbor term under the master lease, the tenant would also lose the rightto renew the master lease 
with respect to the rest of the properties when the initial ten-year lease term ends related to the rest of the properties in 2026. 
In
 connection with the commencement of the third lease year on April 1, 2018, annual rent payments under the master lease increased to $770 million from$757
 million.  Rent  under  the  master  lease  consists  of  a  “base  rent”  component  and  a  “percentage  rent”  component.  As  of  December  31,  2018,  the  base  rentrepresents approximately 90% of the rent payments due under the master lease and the percentage rent represents approximatel
y 10% of the rent payments due underthe
 master lease. The  master lease also provides for fixed annual escalators of 2% on the base rent through the sixth lease year and the possibility for additional 2%increases
 thereafter subject to the tenant meeting an adjusted net revenue to rent ratio, as well as potential increases in percentage rent in year six and every fiveyears
 thereafter based on a percentage of average actual annual net revenue during the preceding five year period calculated in accordance with the terms under themaster lease. 
The  master lease also contains customary events of default and financial covenants. The Company was in compliance with all applicable covenants asof December 31, 2018.
 
Subsequent
 to the Company completing its acquisition of Empire City in January 2019, MGP acquired the developed real property associated with EmpireCity
 from  the  Company  for  consideration  of  approximately  $634  million.  The  real  estate  assets  of  Empire  City  will  be  leased  to  the  Company  pursuant  to  anamendment
 to the master lease, increasing the annual rent payment to MGP by $50 million, prorated for the remainder of the lease year. Consistent with the masterlease
 terms, 90 percent of this rent will be fixed and contractually grow at 2 percent per year until 2022. In addition, the master lease provides the landlord with aright
 of first offer with respect to certain undeveloped land adjacent to the property to the extent the Company develops additional gaming facilities, which thelandlord may exercise shou
ld the Company elect to sell this property in the future.  Additionally, in September 2018, th
e Company entered into a definitive agreement with MGP to acquire Northfield OpCo from MGP for approximately $275million, subject
 to customary purchase price adjustments. The real estate assets of Northfield will be leased to the Company pursuant to an amendment to the masterlease,
 increasing the annual rent payment to MGP by $60 million, prorated for the remainder of the lease year. Consistent with the master lease terms, 90 percent ofthis
 rent will be fixed and contractually grow at 2 percent per year until 2022. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2019, subject to customaryclosing conditions.
 
Also,
 in  December  2018,  the  Company  entered  into  an  agreement  with  MGP  whereby  MGP  will  pay  the  Company  consideration  of  $638  million  forrenovations
 undertaken by the Company regarding the Park MGM and NoMad Las Vegas property (the “Park MGM Lease Transaction”). Additionally, at closing,the parties
 will enter into an amendment to the master lease whereby the annual rent payment to MGP will increase by $50 million, prorated for the remainder of thelease
 year. Consistent with the master lease terms, 90% of this rent will be fixed and contractually grow at 2% per year until 2022. The transaction is expected toclose in the first quar
ter of 2019 and is subject to customary closing conditions.91
 All
 intercompany  transactions,  including  transactions  under  the  master  lease,  have  been  eliminated  in  the  Company’s  consolidation  of  MGP. The  publicownership of MGP’s Class A shares is recognized 
as non-controlling interests in the Com pany’s consolidated financ ial statements.

title: CONDENSED CONSOLIDATING FINANCIAL INFORMATION
heading: NOTE 18 — CONDENSED CONSOLIDATING FINANCIAL INFORMATION
start_phrase: As of December 31, 2018, all of the Company’s principal debt arrangements are guaranteed by each of its material domestic subsidiaries, other than MGPand the Operating Partnership, MGM Grand Detroit, MGM National Harbor, MGM Springfield, and each of their respective subsidiaries.
summary:
- Intercompany transactions, including those under the master lease, are eliminated in consolidation; public ownership of MGM Growth Properties (MGP) Class A shares is recorded as noncontrolling interests.
- Note 18 presents condensed consolidating financial information required for registered debt with subsidiary guarantees:
  - As of December 31, 2018, the Company’s principal debt is guaranteed by its material domestic subsidiaries except MGP and the Operating Partnership, MGM Grand Detroit, MGM National Harbor, MGM Springfield, and their respective subsidiaries. International subsidiaries, including MGM China, are not guarantors.
  - Intercompany cash flow activity is classified as investing when a net intercompany asset exists and as financing when a net intercompany liability exists.
  - Certain subsidiaries hold Operating Partnership units and account for them under the equity method. Due to continuing involvement, the master lease sale-leaseback did not qualify for sale-leaseback accounting; related real estate remains on the MGM subsidiaries’ balance sheets with corresponding finance liabilities for lease payments, and the assets also appear in MGP with eliminations reflected. The Company is reassessing sale recognition and lease classification under ASC 842.
- Condensed consolidating balance sheets are provided as of December 31, 2018 and 2017 across Parent, Guarantor Subsidiaries, MGP, Other, and Elimination columns:
  - Consolidated totals: assets of approximately $30.2 billion (2018) vs. $29.2 billion (2017); liabilities of approximately $19.6 billion (2018) vs. $17.5 billion (2017); total stockholders’ equity of approximately $10.5 billion (2018) vs. $11.6 billion (2017).
- Condensed consolidating statements of operations and comprehensive income for 2018, 2017, and 2016 detail:
  - Consolidated net revenues rising from ~$9.48 billion (2016) to ~$10.80 billion (2017) to ~$11.76 billion (2018).
  - Operating income, interest expense, other income/expense, income taxes, and net income with attribution between MGM Resorts International and noncontrolling interests.
  - Other comprehensive income items include foreign currency translation adjustments and cash flow hedge impacts.
- Condensed consolidating statements of cash flows for 2018, 2017, and 2016 summarize:
  - Operating cash flows (approx. $1.72B in 2018, $2.21B in 2017, $1.53B in 2016).
  - Investing highlights: capital expenditures; acquisitions (e.g., Northfield in 2018; National Harbor in 2017; Borgata in 2016); distributions from unconsolidated affiliates; and intercompany settlements.
  - Financing highlights: bank facility activity; issuances/retirements of debt; MGP public equity offerings (2016, 2017); dividends (including MGP dividends to consolidated subsidiaries); distributions to noncontrolling interests; share repurchases (notably in 2018); and intercompany activity.
- Note 19 provides unaudited selected quarterly financial results for 2018 and 2017 (net revenues, operating income, net income, and EPS by quarter) and explains EPS summation differences due to weighted averages.
  - 2018 comparability items: Q1 Tax Act measurement period tax benefit; Q3 gains on sales of Grand Victoria and Mandarin Oriental; Q4 business interruption insurance proceeds and a Tax Act-related tax expense.
  - 2017 comparability items: Q2 gain from modification of the 2016 NV Energy exit fee and Borgata’s share of an Atlantic City property tax settlement; Q4 large Tax Act-related tax benefit.

As
 of December 31, 2018, all of the Company’s principal debt arrangements are guaranteed by each of its material domestic subsidiaries, other than MGPand
 the  Operating  Partnership,  MGM  Grand  Detroit,  MGM  National  Harbor,  MGM  Springfield,  and  each  of  their  respective  subsidiaries.  The  Company’sinternational
 subsidiaries, including MGM China and its subsidiaries, are not guarantors of such indebtedness. Separate condensed financial statement informationfor
 the subsidiary guarantors and non-guarantors as of December 31, 2018 and 2017 and for the years ended December 31, 2018, 2017 and 2016, are presentedbelow.
 Within the Condensed Consolidating Statements of Cash Flows, the Company has presented net changes in intercompany accounts as investing activities ifthe applicable entities have a
 net asset in intercompany accounts and as a financing activity if the applicable entities have a net intercompany liability balance. 
Certain
 of the Company’s subsidiaries  collectively  own Operating Partnership  units and each subsidiary  accounts for its respective  investment  under theequity
 method  within  the  condensed  consolidating  financial  information  presented  below.  For  these  subsidiaries,  such  investment  constitutes  continuinginvolvement,
 and accordingly, the sale and leaseback of the real estate assets under the master lease do not qualify for sale-leaseback accounting. The real estateassets
 are reflected in the balance sheets of the applicable MGM subsidiaries. In addition, such subsidiaries recognized finance liabilities within “Other long-termobligations” related 
to rent payments due under the master lease and recognized the related interest expense component of such payments. These real estate assets arealso
 reflected on the balance sheet of the MGP subsidiary that received such assets. The condensed consolidating financial information presented below thereforeincludes
 the accounting for such activity within the respective columns presented and in the elimination column. In connection with the adoption of ASC 842, theCompany
 is  reassessing  whether  the  sale  and  leaseback  of  the  real  estate  assets  under  the  master  lease  now  qualify  as  a  passed  sale  and,  accordingly,  thecorresponding lease class
ification, both of which could impact the condensed consolidating financial information.92

9A.
CONTROLS
AND
PROCEDURES  
Disclosure
Controls
and
Procedures
 
Our Chief
 Executive Officer (principal executive officer) and Chief Financial Officer (principal financial officer) have concluded that our disclosure controlsand
 procedures (as defined in Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (“the Exchange Act”)) were effective as ofDecember
 31,  2018  to  provide  reasonable  assurance  that  information  required  to  be  disclosed  in  the  Company’s  reports  under  the  Exchange  Act  is  recorded,processed,
 summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC rules and regulations and to provide that such information is accumulated andcommunicated
 to management to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosures. This conclusion is based on an evaluation as required by Rules 13a-15(b)and
 15d-15(b) under the Exchange Act conducted under the supervision and participation of the principal executive officer and principal financial officer along withcompany management.

in

Control
over

Reporting

s in our internal control over financial reporting that materially affected, or are reasonablylikely to materially affect, our i
nternal control over financial reporting.

Annual
Report
on
Internal
Control
over
Financial
Reporting
 
Management’s
Responsibilities
 
Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting (as defined in Sections 13a-1
5(f) and 15d-15(f)of the Exchange Act) for MGM Resorts In
ternational and subsidiaries (the “Company”). 
Objective
of

o
ver

Reporting

 establishing  adequate  internal  control  over  financial  reporting,  management  has  developed  and  maintained  a  system  of  internal  control,  policies  andprocedures
 designed  to  provide  reasonable  assurance  that  information  contained  in  the  accompanying  consolidated  financial  statements  and  other  informationpresented
 in this annual report is reliable, does not contain any untrue statement of a material fact or omit to state a material fact, and fairly presents in all materialrespects the
 financial condition, results of operations and cash flows of the Company as of and for the periods presented in this annual report. These include controlsand
 procedures designed to ensure that this information is accumulated and communicated to the Company’s management, including its principal executive officerand
 principal financial officer, as appropriate for all timely decisions regarding required disclosure. Significant elements of the Company’s internal control overfinancial reporting 
include, for example: 
• Hiring skilled accounting pe rsonnel and training them appropriately; 
• Written accounting policies;  
• Written documentat ion of accounting systems and procedures; 
• Segregation of incompatib le duties; 
• Internal audit funct ion to monitor the effectiveness of the system of internal control; and 
• Oversight by an independent Audit Commi ttee of the Board of Directors.

mission.

ed above.

ered public accounting firm’s report on the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting appears herein.102

summary:
- The excerpt is Part IV, Item 15 and Item 16 of an annual report (Form 10‑K), detailing financial statements, financial statement schedules, and the exhibits index.
- Financial statements filed under Item 8 include: auditor reports (on consolidated financial statements and on internal control over financial reporting), consolidated balance sheets (Dec 31, 2018 and 2017), statements of operations, comprehensive income (loss), cash flows, stockholders’ equity, and notes for the years ended 2018, 2017, and 2016. Audited consolidated financial statements of CityCenter Holdings, LLC for the same three-year period are incorporated by reference in Exhibit 99.3.
- Financial statement schedule: Schedule II—Valuation and Qualifying Accounts for 2018, 2017, and 2016; all other schedules are omitted as inapplicable or included in the consolidated financial statements/notes.
- Comprehensive exhibits index (many incorporated by reference) covering:
  - Corporate governance documents (amended and restated certificate of incorporation and bylaws).
  - Numerous debt instruments: base indentures and multiple supplemental indentures for Mandalay, MGM Resorts International, and MGM Growth Properties (various senior notes, rates, and maturities), and related guarantees.
  - Registration rights agreement between MGM Growth Properties LLC and MGM Resorts International.
  - Credit agreements and amendments for MGM Resorts International, MGM Growth Properties Operating Partnership LP, and MGM China/MGM Grand Paradise facilities.
  - Macau gaming arrangements: subconcession contract and land concession agreements for MGM Macau.
  - CityCenter Holdings, LLC third amended and restated LLC agreement and related Infinity World stock purchase/support agreements.
  - Master Lease between MGP Lessor, LLC and MGM Lessee, LLC and its amendments.
  - Extensive management/compensatory plans and forms: omnibus incentive plans, performance-based incentive plans, deferred compensation and supplemental executive retirement plans (and amendments), executive employment and separation agreements, director compensation arrangements, RSU/PSU/SAR forms (including profit growth share plan), change-of-control and severance policies, retirement policies, and related employee communications.
  - List of subsidiaries.
  - Consents of Deloitte & Touche LLP (for the company and CityCenter).
  - CEO and CFO certifications under Rules 13a-14(a)/15d-14(a) and Section 1350, with a note that Section 1350 certifications are not deemed filed.
  - Descriptions of operating resorts and of regulation and licensing (Exhibits 99.1 and 99.2).
  - XBRL data files for the consolidated financial statements and financial statement schedule.
- Item 16 (Form 10‑K Summary): None.

- Position and duties: Employee serves as Executive Vice President, General Counsel and Secretary, performing executive, managerial, or administrative duties as specified by Employer. If Employee moves to another Company-affiliated employer during the term, employment with Employer ends and the new affiliate assumes all rights and obligations under the Agreement.
- Term: Fixed term from November 15, 2016 to November 14, 2020 (“Specified Term”). If employment continues past expiration without a new written agreement, employment becomes at-will; only Sections 8, 10.5, 11, and 12 remain in effect. Post-term, Employer may terminate at-will without cause, notice, or severance unless otherwise provided.
- Compensation:
  - Minimum annual salary: $800,000 for years 1–2; $850,000 for years 3–4, paid in arrears on Employer’s regular schedule.
  - Eligibility for generally applicable fringe benefits comparable to similarly situated employees.
  - Reimbursement of reasonable business and travel expenses per Employer policies (as amended from time to time).
  - Performance may be reviewed periodically; consideration for raises, promotions, and participation in discretionary benefit plans is at Employer’s sole discretion.

title: Failure to Satisfy Licensing Requirement
heading: 7. Failure to Satisfy Licensing Requirement.
start_phrase: Employer has the right to terminate Employee’s employment under Section10.1 of this Agreement if: (i) Employee fails to satisfy any licensing requirement referred to in Section 6 above;(ii) Employer is directed to cease business with Employee by any governmental authority referred to in Section 6 above;(iii) Employer determines, in its sole and exclusive judgment, that Employee was, is or might be involved in, or are aboutto be involved in, any activity, relationship(s) or circumstance which could or does jeopardize Employer’s business,reputation or such licenses; or (iv) any of Employer’s licenses is threatened to be, or is, denied, curtailed, suspended orrevoked as a result of Employee’s employment by Employer or as a result of Employee’s actions.
summary:
- The employer operates or may operate in the gaming industry, and the employee must obtain any licenses, qualifications, clearances, or approvals required by the employer or relevant regulatory authorities.
- The employer may terminate employment under Section 10.1 if: (i) the employee fails to meet licensing requirements; (ii) a government authority directs the employer to cease business with the employee; (iii) the employer, in its sole judgment, believes the employee’s activities or relationships could jeopardize the employer’s business, reputation, or licenses; or (iv) the employer’s licenses are threatened, denied, curtailed, suspended, or revoked due to the employee’s employment or actions.
- The agreement includes restrictive covenants recognizing the employee’s access to valuable relationships and Confidential Information, and asserts that post-employment restrictions are necessary to prevent unfair competition.
- In consideration of the agreement and compensation, the employee agrees to heightened protections against misuse or disclosure of Confidential Information and abuse of relationships formed during employment.
- Non-compete (Section 8.1): During the Specified Term and the defined Restrictive Period thereafter, the employee may not directly or indirectly work for, consult with, or be connected to any Competitor in a role that is the same, substantially the same, or similar to roles held with the employer, subject to exceptions referenced in Paragraph 10.
- Key definitions referenced (to be defined in Section 22): Confidential Information, Competitor, and Restrictive Period.

title: Competition
heading: 8.1 Competition.
start_phrase: Except as otherwise explicitly provided in Paragraph 10 of this Agreement, during the entireSpecified Term and thereafter for the “Restrictive Period” (defined below in Section 22) Employee shall notdirectly or indirectly be employed by, provide consultation or other services to, engage in, participate in orotherwise be connected in any way with any “Competitor” (defined below in Section 22)
summary:
- Context: Partial employment agreement for a company engaged in, or applying to engage in, the gaming industry, with heightened regulatory requirements.
- Licensing and regulatory compliance (Sections 6–7):
  - Employee must apply for and obtain any licenses, qualifications, clearances, or approvals required by the Employer or relevant gaming regulators.
  - Employer may terminate employment (per Section 10.1) if: the employee fails to meet licensing requirements; a government authority directs the Employer to cease business with the employee; the Employer believes the employee’s activities could jeopardize its business, reputation, or licenses; or any of the Employer’s licenses are threatened, denied, curtailed, suspended, or revoked due to the employee’s employment or actions.
- Restrictive covenants (Section 8):
  - Non-compete (8.1): During the Specified Term and for a post-employment Restrictive Period (defined in Section 22), the employee may not work for, consult with, or otherwise be connected to a Competitor in a role the same or similar to any role held with the Employer. Exception: if the employee remains at-will after the Specified Term and is later separated for reasons other than Employer’s Good Cause (defined in Section 22), this non-compete does not apply.
  - Non-solicitation and protection of Trade Secrets (8.2): 
    - At all times during and after employment, the employee may not use, access, disclose, or disseminate Company Group Trade Secrets.
    - During employment and for 12 months thereafter, without the Company’s prior written consent, the employee may not: disclose Company Group Business Contacts to Competitors; solicit, induce, or attempt to take away Business Contacts; or approach, solicit, contract with, hire, or entice Business Contacts to end their relationship or employment with the Company Group.
  - Confidentiality (8.3): During and after employment, the employee may not use or disclose Company Group Confidential Information without prior written consent of designated executives (CEO, COO, or General Counsel), with an exception for disclosures required by law or legal process. 
- Definitions referenced but not included: Confidential Information, Restrictive Period, Competitor, Trade Secrets, Business Contacts, Employer’s Good Cause (all in Section 22).

heading: 8.2 Non-Solicitation.

title: Confidentiality
heading: 8.3 Confidentiality.
start_phrase: At all times during Employee's employment with the Company, and at all times thereafter,Employee shall not, without the prior written consent of the Company’s Chief Executive Officer, ChiefOperating Officer or General Counsel in each and every instance--such consent to be within the Company's sole and absolute discretion--use, disclose or make known to any person, entity or other third party outside of theCompany Group any Confidential Information belonging to Company Group or its individual members.
summary:
- Carve-out from Section 8.1: If, after the Specified Term ends, the employee continues at-will and is then separated by the employer during the Restrictive Period for any reason other than Employer’s Good Cause (as defined in Section 22), the employee is not subject to Section 8.1.
- Non-solicitation and trade secret protection (Section 8.2):
  - At all times during and after employment, the employee may not use, access, disclose, or disseminate Company Group Trade Secrets for personal gain or for third parties.
  - During employment and for 12 months thereafter, without the Company’s prior written consent (in its sole discretion), the employee may not:
    - Disclose the Company Group’s Business Contacts to any Competitor or its personnel.
    - Call on, solicit, induce to leave, or take away (or attempt to do so) any Business Contacts.
    - Approach, solicit, contract with, or hire any current Business Contacts, or entice them to end their relationship with or employment by the Company Group.
- Confidentiality (Section 8.3):
  - During and after employment, the employee may not use or disclose any Company Group Confidential Information outside the Company Group without prior written consent from the CEO, COO, or General Counsel (in the Company’s sole discretion).
  - Exceptions: disclosures compelled by law or authority (with 10 days’ advance written notice to allow protective measures), information that becomes public without breach, or information received on a non-confidential basis from a lawful source.
- Third-party information (Section 8.4):
  - The employee must strictly maintain the confidentiality of third parties’ confidential/proprietary information received by the Company Group and use it only as required for job duties and consistent with the Company Group’s agreements, during and after employment.
  - No violation if such information is already public through no wrongful act of the employee or others.
- Ownership and handling of confidential information (Section 8.5):
  - Confidential Information and relationships (including Business Contacts) acquired or developed during employment are the Company’s sole and exclusive property, whether or not they qualify as Trade Secrets.
  - The employee may not store, transfer, maintain, copy, duplicate, or possess Confidential Information on any device or in any format except as expressly approved and issued by the Company, and only with the Company’s express written authorization.

start_phrase: Employee understands and acknowledges that the Company Group has received, andin the future will receive, from third parties, their confidential or proprietary information subject to a duty tomaintain the confidentiality of such information and to use it only for certain limited purposes.
summary:
- Defines exceptions to confidentiality obligations: disclosure compelled by court, arbitration, mediation, or legislative hearing (with 10 days’ prior written notice to allow the Company to seek protective measures); information that becomes public without the employee’s or others’ breach; and information lawfully received on a non-confidential basis from a source entitled to disclose it.
- Imposes strict duties to protect third-party confidential/proprietary information the Company Group receives: keep in strict confidence during and after employment; use only as necessary for job duties and consistent with agreements with those third parties; no violation if the information is already public through no wrongful act.
- Confirms that Confidential Information acquired or developed during employment—including Business Contacts/Relationships developed while employed—is the sole and exclusive property of the Company, whether or not it qualifies as a trade secret.
- Prohibits, during employment, storing, transferring, maintaining, copying, duplicating, or otherwise possessing Confidential Information on any device or in any format except those expressly approved and issued by the Company, absent express written authorization.

start_phrase: Employee understands, agrees, and hereby confirms that Employee's duties andresponsibilities include acquiring Confidential Information and developing Relationships for the benefit ofCompany and, as applicable, Company Group.
summary:
- Exceptions to confidentiality: Employee may disclose Company Confidential Information if legally compelled (e.g., court, arbitration, mediation, or legislative hearing) with 10 days’ prior written notice to allow the Company to seek protection; if it becomes public without breach; or if received lawfully on a non-confidential basis from a third party.
- Third-party information: Employee must keep third-party confidential/proprietary information received by the Company strictly confidential, use it only for permitted purposes during and after employment, and is not liable if the information is already publicly known through no wrongful act.
- Ownership of information and relationships: All Confidential Information and business relationships acquired or developed during employment are the Company’s exclusive property, whether or not they qualify as trade secrets.
- Restrictions on storage/transfer: Employee may not store, copy, transfer, or maintain Confidential Information on any device or in any format unless the device is Company-issued or the action is expressly pre-approved in writing by the Company. A wide range of personal devices and media are expressly covered.
- Return and deletion on separation: Upon termination, Employee must immediately return all Confidential Information, retain no copies, delete any such data from all devices, and, upon request, allow the Company to inspect devices and reasonably access personal computers, email accounts, and devices to verify deletion and non-possession.
- Copyright in compilations: The Company owns copyrights in all compilations of Confidential Information (in any medium). Unauthorized copying, distribution, or derivative works constitute infringement. Only the CEO, COO, President, or General Counsel can authorize such use, and authorization must be in writing in advance. Employee agrees not to challenge the Company’s rights and waives defenses.

title: Severance Payment and COBRA Payment
start_phrase: Employee shall receive an amount equal to: (i) Employee’s annual base salary and (ii) TargetBonus (the “Severance Payment”) (subject to a maximum Severance Payment of $ 4 million) , less all applicable taxes, payable in twelve (12) monthly installments commencing upon the date that isthirty (30) days after the date of separation; plus any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus due toEmployee, payable in accordance with the provisions of the Program.
summary:
- Defines severance benefits upon separation, including:
  - Severance Payment equal to (i) one year of base salary plus (ii) Target Bonus, capped at $4,000,000, less taxes, paid in 12 monthly installments starting 30 days after separation.
  - Payment of any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus per the applicable program.
  - COBRA Payment equal to 1.5 times the cost of 12 months of COBRA coverage, paid in 12 monthly installments starting upon separation.
- Special scenarios:
  - If termination occurs within six months of hire: employee receives only six months of base salary; the restrictive period is limited to six months.

title: Exhibit B - Arbitration
heading: EXHIBIT B - AR B I TRATION
start_phrase: This Exhibit B sets forth the methods for resolving any controversy, dispute or claim directly or indirectly arising out of orrelating to the Employment Agreement (“Agreement”), or the breach thereof, or arising out of or relating to the employmentof Employee, or the termination thereof,
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Establishes binding arbitration as the exclusive method (with limited exceptions) to resolve any controversy, dispute, or claim arising out of or relating to the Employment Agreement, the employee’s employment, or its termination. Becomes part of the Employment Agreement.
- Covered claims: Broadly covers statutory, contractual, tort, and common-law employment claims, including discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, wage and hour, FMLA, ADA, ADEA, Title VII, Section 1981–1988, FLSA, GINA, Nevada employment and civil rights laws, whistleblower, and public policy claims, as well as disputes over compensation, terms, and conditions of employment, and pre-employment statements/actions.
- Parties covered: Applies to claims against the employer, its officers, directors, employees, agents, subsidiaries, divisions, affiliates, successors, and assigns.
- Class/representative action waiver: Employee has no right to bring or arbitrate claims as a class, collective, representative, or private attorney general action.
- Agency filings: Does not preclude filing charges with agencies (e.g., EEOC, NLRB); however, employee waives participation in monetary or other recovery in third-party actions for claims subject to this arbitration agreement.
- Excluded claims: Workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance claims; claims related to employee welfare benefit and pension plans (must use plan procedures); and injunctive or other relief for non-competition and confidentiality violations by either party.
- Non-waiver of substantive rights: Substantive statutory and common-law rights and remedies remain intact; only the judicial forum is waived.
- Time limits and notice: Arbitration must be initiated within the applicable statute of limitations. Written notice describing the claim, facts, and relief sought must be provided within that time frame (to the Employer’s President with a copy to MGM Resorts International’s EVP & General Counsel, or to the employee’s last known address if the employer is the aggrieved party).
- Arbitration forum and selection: Administered by JAMS under its then-current employment arbitration rules. Arbitrator must be a retired judge or experienced employment attorney licensed in the state of arbitration. Selection from a JAMS list of seven neutrals; if no agreement, each party strikes one name and the remaining arbitrator is selected.
- Governing law and procedures: Nevada substantive law (and remedies law), and applicable federal law, govern. Arbitrator cannot apply different substantive law. Non-economic or punitive damages only if authorized by applicable law, with citation required. Privileges apply. Reasonable discovery permitted (written, depositions, subpoenas), disputes on scope decided by arbitrator. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment allowed. Federal Rules of Evidence used. Witness lists exchanged 30 days before hearing; subpoena power available; optional court reporter at a party’s expense. Hearings are private; venue is Las Vegas, Nevada, unless the employee works outside Clark County, in which case venue is in the employee’s county and state of employment.
- Award: Written decision with issues, findings of fact, and conclusions of law; typically issued within 30 days after the hearing or post-hearing briefs. Relief cannot exceed what a court could grant. Award is final and binding; judgment may be entered in court.
- Court involvement: Either party may go to court to compel arbitration or to confirm, enforce, vacate, or modify an award as permitted by law.
- Fees and costs: Employer pays any filing fee and arbitrator’s fees/costs. Each party bears its own attorneys’ fees and litigation expenses, except where a statute or written agreement authorizes fee/cost shifting, in which case the arbitrator may award them under the applicable legal standards.
- Survival and modification: Arbitration provisions survive termination of employment and expiration of the Agreement; they may be modified or revoked only by a signed writing expressly stating that intent.
- No effect on termination provisions: Arbitration terms do not alter the Agreement’s termination provisions. Capitalized terms have the meanings in the Employment Agreement. Severability preserves remaining provisions if any part is unenforceable.
- Acknowledgment: Both parties confirm they have read and understand Exhibit B, agree it is a material employment term, and voluntarily waive a judicial forum (court or jury) for covered claims, without waiving substantive rights. Employee acknowledges the opportunity to consult private legal counsel.
- Signatories indicated: Employee (John M. McManus) and Employer (MGM Resorts International, by James J. Murren, Chairman and CEO).

summary: Exhibit 21 lists MGM Resorts International’s majority-owned subsidiaries as of December 31, 2018, noting that certain minor entities are omitted because, in aggregate, they are not significant. It provides a comprehensive roster spanning operating companies for flagship Las Vegas resorts (Bellagio, Mandalay Bay, The Mirage, New York-New York, CityCenter/Aria/Vdara/The Signature), regional properties (Beau Rivage in Mississippi, MGM Grand Detroit, MGM National Harbor, Borgata/Marina District in New Jersey, MGM Springfield in Massachusetts, Northfield Park and Cedar Downs in Ohio, and Yonkers-related entities in New York), and numerous development, land-holding, leasing, finance, marketing, and corporate service entities. The list also covers the real estate/REIT platform MGM Growth Properties and its GP, operating partnership, finance co-issuer, and lessor entities. International subsidiaries reflect hospitality, branding, marketing, and gaming footprints across Hong Kong, Macau, Mainland China (Beijing), Singapore, India, Japan, Dubai, Isle of Man, Cayman Islands, and the British Virgin Islands, including MGM China Holdings and MGM Asia Pacific. Additional subsidiaries manage arenas and entertainment venues (Las Vegas Arena Management, Park Theater, Grand Garden Arena Management), interactive gaming and sports betting, aviation, manufacturing, insurance, laundry, and retail. Jurisdictions prominently include Nevada, Delaware, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New York, New Jersey, Ohio, and multiple offshore financial and operational hubs. Overall, the exhibit demonstrates MGM’s vertically integrated structure across operations, development, branding, international expansion, and real estate financing.

heading: Exhibit 31.1 CERTIFICATION
start_phrase: I have reviewed this annual report on Form 10-K of MGM Resorts International;
summary:
- Exhibit 31.1: CEO certification for MGM Resorts International’s annual report on Form 10-K, consistent with Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302.
- James J. Murren certifies he reviewed the report; it contains no untrue statements or omissions of material fact; and the financial statements fairly present the company’s financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows.
- Affirms responsibility, with the other certifying officer, for establishing and maintaining disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting in accordance with Exchange Act Rules 13a-15 and 15d-15.
- Actions taken include:
  - Designing disclosure controls to ensure material information, including from consolidated subsidiaries, is made known during report preparation.
  - Designing internal control over financial reporting to provide reasonable assurance of reliable GAAP-compliant reporting.
  - Evaluating the effectiveness of disclosure controls and presenting conclusions in the report.
  - Disclosing any changes in internal control over financial reporting during the most recent fiscal quarter that materially affected or are reasonably likely to materially affect such controls.
- Confirms disclosure to auditors and the audit committee of all significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting, and any fraud (material or not) involving management or employees with significant control responsibilities.
- Dated February 27, 2019, signed by James J. Murren, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer.

  - All significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in ICFR reasonably likely to affect the company’s ability to record, process, summarize, and report financial information.

title: Exhibit 99.1 Description of Our Operating Resorts
heading: Exhibit 99.1 DESCRIPTION OF OUR OPERATING RESORTS
start_phrase: The following information des cribes each of our operating resorts, including their key amenities, features and awards.
summary:
- Purpose: Exhibit 99.1 provides an overview of the company’s operating resorts, highlighting locations, awards, signature amenities, dining, entertainment, retail, meeting/convention space, and unique attractions.

- Las Vegas Strip portfolio:
  - Bellagio: AAA Five Diamond; iconic fountains and seasonal conservatory; fine dining (Picasso, Le Cirque); spa, pool, Gallery of Fine Art; Via Bellagio luxury retail; Cirque du Soleil’s “O”; connections to Vdara and Crystals.
  - MGM Grand Las Vegas: AAA Four Diamond; StayWell rooms, Skylofts (AAA Five Diamond), The Mansion; The Signature all‑suite non‑gaming; celebrity dining (including Joël Robuchon, Michelin three‑star); entertainment (KÀ by Cirque du Soleil, MGM Grand Garden Arena, David Copperfield, Brad Garrett’s Comedy Club); nightlife (Hakkasan, Wet Republic); extensive meeting space and trade show pavilion; wedding chapel, pool/spa.
  - Mandalay Bay: AAA Four Diamond; restaurants by noted chefs; multiple venues (12,000‑seat arena, House of Blues, Michael Jackson ONE by Cirque); 2.1M sq ft of convention space; Shark Reef Aquarium; expansive beach/pool complex with concerts, Moorea and Daylight Beach Club; Spa Mandalay; includes Four Seasons (AAA Five Diamond) and Delano (with Rivea and Skyfall by Alain Ducasse).
  - The Mirage: AAA Four Diamond; erupting volcano, tropical atrium; Secret Garden and Dolphin Habitat; dining; entertainment (The Beatles LOVE by Cirque, Terry Fator, Aces of Comedy); nightlife (1OAK, Parlor); retail and 170,000 sq ft of meetings/convention space.
  - Luxor: Pyramid with signature light beam; meeting space, spa; dining (TENDER, Public House, Diablo’s Cantina); attractions (Titanic: The Artifact Exhibition, Bodies…The Exhibition); shows (Blue Man Group, Carrot Top, Fantasy).
  - Excalibur: Castle‑themed; shows (Tournament of Kings, The Australian Bee Gees, Thunder from Down Under); attractions (Fun Dungeon arcade, Castle Walk); multiple dining venues; fitness/spa and large pool deck; tram connection to Luxor and Mandalay Bay.
  - New York‑New York: NYC‑themed skyline, roller coaster; dining (Tom’s Urban, Shake Shack, Nine Fine Irishmen); entertainment (Zumanity by Cirque, Times Square piano bar); connected to Park MGM and T‑Mobile Arena via The Park.
  - Park MGM (with NoMad): Dining (Bavette’s, Primrose) and Eataly market; Park Theater (5,200 seats) for headliners; NoMad Hotel features boutique hospitality and Jacques Garcia design.

- Additional U.S. resorts:
  - Circus Circus Las Vegas: Adventuredome indoor theme park, Midway; THE Steak House; Splash Zone water amenities.
  - MGM Grand Detroit: Downtown integrated resort; dining (Wolfgang Puck Steak, TAP); nightlife, spa; 30,000 sq ft of meeting space.
  - Beau Rivage (Biloxi): Beachfront; remodeled rooms; multiple restaurants/bars; 1,550‑seat theatre; upscale retail promenade; spa/salon; 50,000 sq ft of convention space.
  - Gold Strike Tunica: Dockside casino near Memphis; Millennium Theatre; dining; 20,000 sq ft meeting space; part of a three‑casino complex.
  - Borgata (Atlantic City): Extensive gaming; restaurants (Angeline, Bobby Flay Steak, Izakaya, Wolfgang Puck); retail; spa; ~70,000 sq ft of meeting space; Water Club (18,000 sq ft events); Music Box (1,000 seats).
  - MGM National Harbor (MD/DC): Boutique hotel; celebrity chef dining (José Andrés, Voltaggio brothers); 3,000‑seat theater; seasonal conservatory; bars/lounges; 27,000‑sq‑ft spa/salon; curated retail (incl. SJP boutique).
  - MGM Springfield (MA): Downtown resort with locally inspired design; chef‑driven restaurants; lounges; cinema and bowling; spa, pool; 34,000 sq ft of convention space; manages adjacent MassMutual Center (8,000 seats; 100,000 sq ft meetings).

- Macau properties:
  - MGM Macau: Five‑star integrated resort on Macau Peninsula; Grande Praça atrium; rooms/suites/villas; diverse dining; pool/spa; direct connection to One Central luxury retail.
  - MGM Cotai: Award‑winning integrated resort on the Cotai Strip; rooms/suites; meeting space; spa; retail; F&B; The Mansion luxury experience; Asia’s first dynamic theater and innovative spectacle.

- Common themes across properties: industry recognitions (AAA, Michelin), Cirque du Soleil and headline entertainment, celebrity chef dining, expansive meeting/convention facilities, luxury spas and pools, distinctive retail, and unique, destination‑defining attractions with inter‑property connectivity in Las Vegas.

The following information des
cribes each of our operating resorts, including their key amenities, features and awards.Bellagio
Bellagio
 is  located  at  the  heart  of  the  Las  Vegas  Strip  and  has  earned  the  prestigious  Five  Diamond  award  from  the  American  Automobile  Association(“AAA”)
 since 2001.  The resort is richly decorated, including a conservatory filled with unique botanical displays that change with the seasons.  At the front ofBellagio
 is  an  eight-acre  lake  featuring  over  1,000  fountains  that  come  alive  at  regular  intervals  in  a  choreographed  ballet  of  water,  music  and  lights.  For  bothbusiness
 and leisure customers, Bellagio’s restaurants offer the finest choices, including Five Diamond award winners Picasso and Le Cirque.  Leisure travelers canalso enjoy Bellagio’s expansiv
e pool, world-class spa and Gallery of Fine Arts.  Via Bellagio features luxury retail shops and restaurants.  Bellagio
 features O,
 the Cirque du Soleil production where world-class acrobats, synchronized swimmers, divers and characters perform in, on, and abovewater. 
 Other entertainment options include Hyde Lounge overlooking the Bellagio fountains and several other unique bars and lounges.  Bellagio is connected via acovered walkway with Vdara and by a peopl
e mover to Crystals.MGM
Grand
Las
Vegas
MGM
 Grand Las Vegas, located on the corner of the Las Vegas Strip and Tropicana Avenue is a recipient of the prestigious AAA Four Diamond award.  Inaddition to the standard room offerings, the resort also offers several unique room offerings, incl
uding: StayWell, a unique wellness hotel experience; Skylofts, ultra-luxurious
 penthouse  suites  featuring  the ultimate  in personal  service  and a AAA Five Diamond award winner;  and the exclusive  Mansion for premium  gamingcustomers.  Additionally, The Signa
ture at MGM Grand is a connecting AAA Four Star all-suite, non-smoking, non-gaming development featuring three towers.The
 resort boasts an extensive array of restaurants including two restaurants by renowned chef Joël Robuchon – whose self-titled restaurant is a AAA FiveDiamond
 award recipient and a recipient of a Michelin three-star rating.  Other celebrity chef restaurants include Craftsteak by Tom Colicchio, Michael Mina’s Pub1842, Emeril Lagasse’s New Orleans Fish House, and Hakk
asan.MGM
 Grand offers unique entertainment options including the spectacular show KÀ
 , by Cirque du Soleil, performed in a custom-designed theatre seatingalmost
 2,000  guests.   The  MGM  Grand  Garden  Arena,  with  a  seating  capacity  of  over  16,000,  hosts  premier  concerts,  award  shows,  sporting  events  includingchampionship boxing, and other spec
ial events.  The David Copperfield Theatre and Brad Garrett’s Comedy Club entertain guests seven nights a week.  For
 Daylife and Nightlife club goers, Hakkasan Las Vegas is the ultimate mega-night club and Wet Republic is the ultra-pool dayclub with shared globalsuperstar resident DJs.  
Other
 amenities include a traditional Wedding Chapel, numerous retail shopping outlets, over 800,000 square feet of flexible meeting space, a 90,000 squarefoot pillar-less tr
ade show pavilion, and an extensive pool and spa complex.Mandalay
Bay
Mandalay
 Bay is the first major resort on the Las Vegas Strip to greet visitors arriving by automobile from Southern California.  This AAA Four Diamondresort
 features  numerous  restaurants,  such  as  Charlie  Palmer's  Aureole,  Wolfgang  Puck's  Lupo,  Hubert  Keller’s  Fleur,  Shawn  McClain’s  Libertine  Social  andMichael Mina’s Stripsteak.  Mandalay Bay offers multiple entertainment venues that incl
ude a 12,000-seat special events arena, the House of Blues, and a 1,700-seatshowroom which is the home of the 
Cirque
du
Soleil
 Michael Jackson ONE production show. Mandalay
 Bay also offers 2.1 million square feet of convention, ballroom and meeting rooms.  At the south end of the convention center is the Shark ReefAquarium,
 exhibiting  sharks,  other  fascinating  sea  creatures  and  a  Komodo  dragon.   Mandalay  Bay’s  expansive  pool  and  beach  area  plays  host  to  an  array  ofevening
 open air concerts during the pool season, a large wave pool, and Moorea, a European-style “ultra” beach and Daylight Beach Club.  The resort also featuresSpa Mandalay, a 30,000 square-foot spa 
and fitness center.Included
 within Mandalay Bay is a Four Seasons Hotel with its own lobby, restaurants and pool and spa, providing visitors with 14 years of AAA Five-Diamond-rated
 hospitality  experience.   The Delano is an all-suite  hotel  tower within the Mandalay Bay complex.   The Delano includes its own spa and fitnesscenter, a lounge and rest
aurants, including Rivea and the Skyfall lounge, created by famed chef Alain Ducasse and located on the top floor of The Delano. 
 The
Mirage
The
 Mirage  is a  tropically-themed  hotel  and  casino  resort  located  at  the  center  of  the  Las  Vegas  Strip  and  is  recognized  by  AAA  as  a  Four  Diamondresort.
  The exterior of the resort is landscaped with lagoons and other water features centered around a volcano that erupts at scheduled intervals.  Inside the frontentrance
 is an atrium with a tropical garden and additional water features capped by a 100-foot-high glass dome.  Located at the rear of the hotel, adjacent to theswimming
 pool area, is Siegfried 
&
Roy’s
Secret
Garden
and
Dolphin
Habitat
,  an attraction featuring bottlenose dolphins that allow guests to view the beautifulexotic animals of Siegf
ried & Roy, the world-famous illusionists.The Mirage
 features a wide array of restaurants, including Tom Colicchio’s Heritage Steak, Stack and Osteria Costa.  Casual dining options include CravingsBuffet, Carnegie Deli, Califo
rnia Pizza Kitchen and Pantry.  Entertainment at The Mirage features The Beatles Love, by Cirque du Soleil; celebrity impressionist andventriloquist
 Terry Fator, winner of NBC’s America’s Got Talent competition; and The Mirage Aces of Comedy series featuring acts such as Daniel Tosh, RonWhite,
 Ray Romano and others.  Nightlife options at The Mirage include 1OAK night club and Parlor, an intimate piano lounge.  The Mirage has numerous retailshopping outlets and 170,000 square fee
t of meetings and convention space, including the 90,000-square foot Mirage Events Center.Luxor
Luxor
 is a pyramid-shaped hotel and casino resort situated at the south end of the Las Vegas strip between Mandalay Bay and Excalibur.  In addition to thewell-known beam
 of light, brilliantly shining from the top of the pyramid, Luxor offers over 35,000 square feet of flexible meeting space, Nurture Spa, and food andentertainment
 venues on three different levels beneath a soaring hotel atrium.  Nightlife and dining at Luxor includes TENDER steak & seafood, rated one of LasVegas’
 top steakhouses, Public House, the popular East Coast hangout featuring casual cocktails, comfortable food and spectacular sports and Diablo’s Cantina, arestaurant featuring a unique brand of south-of-the-border dining.  The Luxor is home
 to Titanic:

and Bodies…

.  With some of
 the most popular entertainment in Las Vegas, Luxor features the popular entertainment show Blue Man Group, “Entertainer of the Year” prop comic Carrot
Top and the adult dance revue

 . Excalibur
Excalibur
 is  a  castle-themed  hotel  and  casino  complex  situated  immediately  north  of  Luxor  at  the  corner  of  Las  Vegas  Boulevard  and  TropicanaAvenue.  Entertainment options
 at Excalibur include the long-running Tournament
of

 dinner show, The

 and the male revue Thunder
from Down

.   Excalibur’s other world-class venues include the Fun Dungeon, featuring the Excalibur arcade, and the Castle Walk, a shopping expedition featuringartisans’

m allowing guests to travel easily from resort to resort.New
York-New
York
New
 York-New York is located at the corner of the Las Vegas Strip and Tropicana Avenue.  Pedestrian bridges link New York-New York with both MGMGrand
 Las Vegas and Excalibur.  The architecture at New York-New York replicates many of New York City’s landmark buildings and icons, including the Statueof

include Zumanity
 by  Cirque du Soleil and The Bar at Times Square piano bar. New York-New York, Park MGM and the T-Mobile Arena areconnected by The Park, an ecle
ctic blend of restaurants, bars, and entertainment.  Park
MGM
Park

 at Bavette’s Steakhouse & Bar and Primrose. Park MGM also features Eataly, a vibrant market with cafes, to-go counters and restaurants interspersed withhigh-quality
 products from sustainable Italian and local producers. Park MGM is also home to the Park Theater, which opened in December 2016. The 5,200 seat-entertainment venue was

 in Park MGM is NoMad Hotel, a placed of rendezvous and romance, where elegant evenings and moments of chance mix with extraordinary foodand

Las

ing and events space.Beau

ated by unaffiliated third parties.  Borgata

are feet of event space and The Music Box, a concert venue with 1,000 seats.  National

heading: Exhibit 99.2 DESCRIPTION OF REGULATION AND LICENSING
start_phrase: The gaming industry is highly regulated, and we must maintain our licenses and pay gaming taxes to continue our operations.
summary: Exhibit 99.2 details the extensive regulatory and licensing framework governing MGM Resorts’ gaming operations across multiple jurisdictions, emphasizing strict suitability, reporting, ownership, and taxation requirements and the risk that violations or regulatory changes could materially affect operations. In Nevada, the Nevada Gaming Commission, Control Board, and local authorities license MGM’s casino and manufacturer/distributor subsidiaries, regulate public company registrations (including Mandalay Resort Group and Mirage Resorts, Incorporated), require suitability for officers, directors, key employees, significant security holders and in some cases debt holders, impose ownership thresholds (>5% reporting; >10% suitability; institutional investor waivers up to 25%–29% for investment-only), mandate approvals for financings, public offerings, and control changes, and levy taxes/fees including a 6.75% tax on gross gaming revenues and a live entertainment tax; a $10,000 foreign-gaming revolving fund and local alcoholic-beverage licensing also apply. In Michigan, MGM Grand Detroit operates under the Michigan Gaming Control and Revenue Act and the Michigan Gaming Control Board, with annual casino licensure based on integrity and financial suitability, supplier and occupational licensing, acquisition approval for holdings >5% (institutional waivers with notice and filing thresholds), Detroit development-agreement compliance reporting, liquor control oversight, and prior approval for debt transactions; taxes/fees include a 19% wagering tax, a municipal service fee equal to the greater of $4 million or 1.25% of adjusted gross receipts, an annual assessment of approximately $8.3 million (CPI-adjusted), and a 1%–2% payment to Detroit based on adjusted gross receipts. In Mississippi, Beau Rivage and Gold Strike Tunica are licensed by the Mississippi Gaming Commission, which enforces suitability (including work permits), shareholder thresholds (>5% reporting; >10% suitability; institutional investor waivers up to 25%–29%), approvals for securities offerings, pledges, guarantees, and control changes, corporate defense oversight, foreign-gaming approvals, and penalties including fines, supervision, suspension, or revocation; taxes/fees include an 8% state fee on gross revenues (creditable against income tax) plus about 4% local fees, with infrastructure requirements (e.g., 500-car parking and resort amenities) and 24-hour alcohol service in designated resort areas subject to licensing of key owners/officers. In Macau, MGM Grand Paradise’s subconcession (governing MGM Macau and MGM Cotai) requires government approvals for share transfers and control changes (including indirect holdings at or above 5%), prohibits delegation of gaming management, mandates suitability for shareholders ≥5% and directors/key employees with sanctions for unsuitability, and requires approvals for recapitalizations and potential capital increases; the subconcession expires March 31, 2020 (subject to possible redemption with compensation or unilateral termination for fundamental non-compliance), and imposes operational covenants, reporting, and insurance. Macau taxes/fees include an annual premium (fixed 30 million patacas plus variable amounts per table/machine, minimum 45 million), a 35% special gaming tax on gross gaming revenues plus 1.6% and 2.4% levies, with no deduction for credit losses; land concessions for MGM Macau and MGM Cotai run to 2031 and 2038 (renewable), and casino gaming profits have been exempt from Macau corporate income tax through March 31, 2020. The company is also subject to non-gaming laws (e.g., alcohol, smoking, environmental, employment/immigration, currency transactions, taxation, zoning/building, land use, marketing/advertising, timeshare, lending, privacy/telemarketing, OFAC, FCPA, and anti–money laundering).

The

In

Government
Regulation
 
The

The

Any change in the laws, regulations, 
and supervisory procedures of the Nevada Gaming Authorities could have an adverse effect on our gaming operations. 
Each

urer and distributor licensees, and the foregoing subsidiaries are collectively referred to as the “Nevada licensed subsidiaries.”

 corporations”) and Mirage Resorts, Incorporated is required to be registered as an intermediary company and, as such, each of us is required periodicallyto submit detailed financial
 and operating reports to the Nevada Commission and furnish any other information that the Nevada Commission may require. No personmay become a stockholder or

 all  persons  owning  or  controlling  the  stock  of  any  corporation  controlling  a  gaming  licensee.  The  Nevada  registered  corporations,  Mirage  Resorts,Incorporated

The

eview in Nevada.

Any beneficial

ion.

cumstances, own up to 29% of the voting securities of a registered company for a limited period of time and maintain the waiver.

ct to the Nevada Act. However, to date, the Nevada Commission has not imposed such a requirement on the Nevada registered corporations.

es. An approval, if given, does not

Changes

r Nevada’s policy to:

rol of that corporation. 
License
 fees and taxes, computed in various ways depending on the type of gaming or activity involved, are payable to the State of Nevada and to the localauthorities. Depending upon the pa
rticular fee or tax involved, these fees and taxes are payable either monthly, quarterly, or annually and are based upon either:

Because

lity, or who has been found guilty of cheating at gambling.

 sale of alcoholic beverages by the Nevada licensed subsidiaries is subject to licensing, control, and regulation by the applicable local authorities. Alllicenses

and

The
 Michigan  Gaming  Control  and  Revenue  Act  (the  “Michigan  Act”)  subjects  the  owners  and  operators  of  casino  gaming  facilities  to  extensive  statelicensing
 and regulatory requirements. The Michigan Act also authorizes local regulation of casino gaming facilities by the City of Detroit, provided that any suchlocal

it, LLC (the “licensed subsidiary”) which operates MGM Grand Detroit. Our ownership interest in MGM Grand Detroit,LLC is held by our wholly-owned subsidiary MGM Grand Detroi
t, Inc. 
The
 Michigan Act creates the Michigan Gaming Control Board (the “Michigan Board”) and authorizes it to grant casino licenses to not more than threeapplicants
 who  have  entered  into  development  agreements  with  the  City  of  Detroit.  The  Michigan  Board  is  granted  extensive  authority  to  conduct  backgroundinvestigations and determine the suitability of casino license applicants, affiliated companies, officers, directors, or managerial employees of applicants and affiliated
companies and
 persons or entities holding a one percent or greater direct or indirect interest in an applicant or affiliated company. Institutional investors holding lessthan
 certain specified amounts of our debt or equity securities are exempted from meeting the suitability requirements of the Michigan Act since we are a publiclytraded
 corporation, and provided that the securities were purchased for investment purposes only and not for the purpose of influencing or affecting our affairs. Anyperson
 who supplies goods or services to the licensed subsidiary which are directly related to, used in connection with, or affecting gaming, and any person whosupplies
 other goods or services to the licensed subsidiary on a regular and continuing basis, must obtain a supplier’s license from the Michigan Board. In addition,any
 individual employed by the licensed subsidiary or by a supplier licensee whose work duties are related to or involved in the gaming operation or are performedin a restricted ar
ea or a gaming area of the licensed subsidiary must obtain an occupational license from the Michigan Board. 
The
 Michigan Act imposes the burden of proof on the applicant for a casino license to establish its suitability to receive and hold the license. The applicantmust
 establish  its  suitability  as  to  integrity,  moral  character  and  reputation,  business  probity,  financial  ability  and  experience,  responsibility,  and  other  criteriadeemed
 appropriate by the Michigan Board. A casino license is valid for a period of one year and the Michigan Board may refuse to renew it upon a determinationthat the licensee no long
er meets the requirements for licensure. 
The
 Michigan Board may, among other things, revoke, suspend or restrict the licensed subsidiary’s casino license. The licensed subsidiary is also subject tofines

 than 120 days, the Michigan Act provides for the appointment of a conservator who, among other things, is required to preserve the assets to ensure that theyshall

rements of the Michigan Act for licensure, subject to certain approvals and consultations. 
The
 Michigan Board has adopted administrative  rules to implement the terms of the Michigan Act. Among other things, the rules impose more detailedsubstantive and procedural 
requirements with respect to casino licensing and operations.

cants for or holders of casino licenses. 
Under

 the Michigan Board for approval of the acquisition within 45 days after it occurs. The institutional investor and its key persons may be subject to suitabilityand qualification det
erminations. 
The
 term “institutional investor” includes financial institutions, insurance companies, pension funds, mutual funds, etc. The shares held by the institutionalinvestor must

oses andnot to cause a change in its

The
 Michigan  Liquor  Control  Commission  licenses,  controls  and  regulates  the  sale  of  alcoholic  beverages  by  the  licensed  subsidiary  pursuant  to  theMichigan

The
 Detroit City Council enacted an ordinance entitled “Casino Gaming Authorization and Casino Development Agreement Certification and Compliance.”The
 ordinance authorizes casino gaming only by operators who are licensed by the Michigan Board and are parties to a development agreement which has beenapproved
 and certified by the City Council and is currently in effect, or are acting on behalf of such parties. The development agreement among the City of Detroit,MGM Grand Detroit, LLC and the Economic Develop
ment Corporation of the City of Detroit has been so approved and certified and is currently in effect. Under theordinance,
 the  licensed  subsidiary  is  required  to  submit  to  the  Mayor  of  Detroit  and  to  the  City  Council  periodic  reports  regarding  its  compliance  with  thedevelopment
 agreement or, in the event of non-compliance, reasons for non-compliance and an explanation of efforts to comply. The ordinance requires the Mayorof
 Detroit to monitor each casino operator’s compliance with its development agreement, to take appropriate enforcement action in the event of default and to notifythe
 City Council of defaults and enforcement action taken; and, if a development agreement is terminated, it requires the City Council to transmit notice of suchaction
 to the Michigan Board within five business days along with Detroit’s request that the Michigan Board revoke the relevant operator’s casino license. If adevelopment agreemen
t is terminated, the Michigan Act requires the Michigan Board to revoke the relevant operator’s casino license upon the request of Detroit. 
The
 administrative rules of the Michigan Board prohibit the licensed subsidiary or us from entering into a debt transaction affecting the capitalization orfinancial viabili
ty of MGM Grand Detroit without prior approval from the Michigan Board. 
The Michigan
 Act effectively provides for a wagering tax equal to 19% of adjusted gross receipts from gaming operations conducted at a casino. Proceeds ofthe wagering tax
 are shared between the State of Michigan and the City of Detroit. In addition to the wagering tax, the Michigan Act establishes an annual municipalservice
 fee equal to the greater of $4 million or 1.25% of adjusted gross receipts to be paid to Detroit to defray its cost of hosting casinos, and an annual assessment,as
 adjusted  annually  based  upon  a  consumer  price  index,  in  the  initial  amount  of  approximately  $8.3  million  to  be  paid  to  Michigan  to  defray  its  regulatoryenforcement
 and  other  casino-related  costs.  These  payments  are  in  addition  to  the  taxes,  fees  and  assessments  customarily  paid  by  business  entities  situated  inDetroit.
 The licensed subsidiary is also obligated to pay 1% of its adjusted gross receipts to Detroit, to be increased to 2% of its adjusted gross receipts in anycalendar year in which ad
justed gross receipts exceed $400 million.

ject to certain reporting requirements to the Macau gaming authorities. 
 
12

 Under
 the subconcession, MGM Grand Paradise Limited is obligated to pay to the Macau S.A.R. an annual premium with a fixed portion and a variableportion
 based on the number and type of gaming tables employed and gaming machines operated. The fixed portion of the premium is equal to 30 mil lion patacas (approximately
 $3.83  million,  based on exchange rates at December   31 , 201 8 ). The variable  portion  is equal  to 300,000 patacas  per gaming table  reservedexclusively
 for certain kinds of games or players, 150,000 patacas per gaming table not so reserved and 1,000 patacas per electrical or mechanical gaming machine,including
 slot machines (approximately $ 38,304 ,  $ 19,152 and  $12 8 , respectively, based on exchange rates at December  31 , 201 8 ), subject to a minimum offorty five million pa
tacas (approximately $5. 75  million, based on exchange rates at December  31 , 201 8 ). MGM Grand Paradise Limited also has to pay a specialgaming
 tax  of  35%  of  gross  gaming  revenues  and  applicable  withholding  taxes.  It  must  also  contribute  1.6%  and  2.4%  (a  portion  of  which  must  be  used  forpromotion
 of  tourism  in  Macau)  of  its  gross  gaming  revenue  to  a  public  foundation  designated  by  the  Macau  S.A.R.  government  and  to  the  Macau  S.A.R,respectively, as speci
al levy. 
Currently,
 the gaming tax in Macau is calculated as a percentage of gross gaming revenue. However, gross gaming revenue does not include deductions forcredit
 losses. As a result, if MGM Grand Paradise issues markers to its customers in Macau and is unable to collect on the related receivables from them, it has topay taxes on its winnings from thes
e customers even though it was unable to collect the related receivables. 
MGM
 Grand Paradise has received a concession from the Macau government to use a 10.67 acre parcel of land for MGM Macau (the “MGM Macau LandContract”). The land concess
ion will expire on April 6, 2031 and is renewable. 
The
 MGM Macau Land Contract requires MGM Grand Paradise to pay a premium which was paid in full before the opening of MGM Macau. In addition,MGM Grand Paradise
 is also obligated to pay rent annually for the term of the MGM Macau Land Contract. The rent amount may be revised every five years by theMacau government, accord
ing to the provisions of the Macau Land law. 
In addition,
 MGM Grand Paradise has received a concession from the Macau government to use an approximately 18 acre site in Cotai Macau and develop asecond resort and casino (th
e “MGM Cotai Land Contract”). The land concession will expir e on January 8, 2038 and is renewable. 
The
 MGM Cotai Land Contract requires MGM Grand Paradise to pay a premium, which was paid in full before the opening of MGM Cotai. In addition,MGM
 Grand Paradise is also obligated to pay rent annually for the term of the MGM Cotai Land Contract. The rent amount may be revised every five years by theMacau government, accord
ing to the provisions of the Macau Land law. 
MGM
 Grand Paradise received an exemption from Macau’s corporate income tax on profits generated by the operation of casino games of chance for aperiod of
 five-years starting at January 1, 2007. In October 2011, MGM Grand Paradise was granted an extension of this exemption for an additional five years. Theexemption was further ext
ended on September 7, 2016 through March 31, 2020.
